The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1294 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • According to recent reports, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • In a recent development, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

According to recent reports, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

In a recent development, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to promptly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Industry observers note that microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed patch in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

It has been revealed that external pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

It has been revealed that “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar problems elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

It has been revealed that matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These fresh threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

It has been revealed that still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

Sources indicate that in the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the tech giant that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are vital nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik claims. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

In a recent development, only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

Sources indicate that “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

Recent findings suggest that • Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some tech giant data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

Industry observers note that • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech tech giant was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

Tech Report: NASA+ Documentary Captures Europa Clipper’s Journey Into Deep Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”.
  • According to recent reports, the documentary will air on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov.
  • It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA invites the world behind the scenes to witness the story of Europa Clipper’s journey from a far-off vision to a cutting-edge deep space exploration mission with the release of the agency’s newest documentary, “The Europa Concept.”.

According to recent reports, the documentary will air on NASA+, the NASA app, and the agency’s website starting Monday, Nov. 23, and is coming soon to YouTube.

It took decades of science, thousands of dedicated minds, endless creativity, and a whole lot of grit to get the Europa Clipper spacecraft to the launch pad in 2024. Now the orbiter, the largest NASA has ever sent into deep space, is two years into its five-year, 1.8 billion-mile (2.9 billion-kilometer) journey to the Jupiter system, where it will conduct flybys of Europa in search of the conditions for life in the vast ocean thought to hide beneath the moon’s icy surface.

It has been revealed that “The things we will learn from Europa Clipper will be so sensational, so fantastic, that everyone will be screaming for the next mission,” remarked Curt Niebur, program scientist in the Planetary Science Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “The only thing that matters is that we learn enough that we, in the broadest sense, want to do it again somewhere else — because that’s what exploration is.”.

Following a team of dedicated engineers and scientists on their yearslong efforts, the documentary captures how they developed a mission to Europa and built a spacecraft capable of surviving one of the most punishing radiation environments in our solar system. A product of Jupiter’s powerful magnetic field, that same radiation may have contributed to creating a potentially habitable environment on Europa.

It has been revealed that the moon, an object of fascination since its discovery by Galileo Galilei in 1610, only began to reveal its secrets with data obtained by NASA’s Pioneer 10 in 1973, followed the next year by Pioneer 11. But humanity didn’t get its first detailed look at Europa until Voyager 1’s flyby in 1979. More detailed glimpses of the moon followed from the agency’s Voyager 2, Galileo, Cassini, and Juno missions, each helping illuminate the way for Europa Clipper.

Work officially began on the mission at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California in 2013, initiating an 11-year trek to build the spacecraft and its suite of nine science instruments in time to launch during a specific period of planetary alignment. Along the way, the team encountered plenty of unforeseen challenges, including a global pandemic and, just before launch on Oct. 14, 2024, a Category 5 hurricane and tornadoes near NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

Sources indicate that “With Europa Clipper, we’ve taken the next step in solar system exploration, which will help us uncover the mysteries of an ocean world, and ultimately, whether potentially habitable worlds beyond our own exist,” remarked Jordan Evans, director of flight projects at JPL and the mission’s previous project manager. “This documentary pays tribute to the ingenuity, teamwork, and dedication that continue to make this incredible mission possible.”.

“The Europa Concept” takes audiences through the highs and lows alongside the thousands more who made Europa Clipper’s journey to the launch pad a success — and who will, in the coming years, be there to share the mission’s findings about humanity’s place in the cosmos.

Find “The Europa Concept” on NASA+ here:.

https://plus.nasa.gov/video/the-europa-concept/.

Sources indicate that managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California, JPL leads the development of the Europa Clipper mission in partnership with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, for NASA. The main spacecraft body was designed by APL in collaboration with JPL and NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, and NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The Planetary Missions Program Office at NASA Marshall executes program management of the Europa Clipper mission. NASA’s Launch Services Program, based at Kennedy, managed the launch service for the Europa Clipper spacecraft.

Find more information about Europa Clipper here:.

https://science.nasa.gov/mission/europa-clipper/.

Industry News: How This Year’s Super El Niño Will Worsen Global Hunger

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
  • It has been revealed that the world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought.
  • The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story originally appeared on Yale E360 and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

It has been revealed that the world is now in the grip of a super El Niño: a Godzilla-sized version of a natural climate phenomenon that has already shriveled rivers, upended aquaculture, and flattened crops with drought. But the global organizations that keep an eye on food security are warning of even tougher times ahead.

The impacts of an El Niño can be far-reaching and catastrophic. In the late 19th century, one of the strongest El Niños on record helped to fuel multiyear droughts across Asia, Brazil, and Africa that spurred a global famine: Some 50 million people, or 3 percent of the global population, died. Thankfully, the ways we blueprint for bad weather and move food around the planet have improved massively since then, with organizations working hard to provide relief where it’s needed. But the impacts of bad weather on crops are still hard to avoid. After a strong El Niño hit in 2015, cereal yields across Southern Africa were 20 percent below normal; crop yields in parts of Ethiopia dropped by 90 percent.

It has been revealed that this year’s El Niño has already, by one measure, topped those previous record holders in strength. And it’s still growing. By the time the phenomenon peaks in early winter, sea-surface warming in the tropical Pacific could be higher than anything seen in a millennium. In August, the World Food Programme warned that this El Niño might push an additional 49 million people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, taking the total number to 274 million. Worryingly, this year’s event comes as global aid dollars are pinched and wars are making it hard to plug holes in global food systems.

“It’s a triple whammy of high fertilizer costs, high energy costs, and now massive droughts across the tropics,” states Berkeley Earth climatologist Zeke Hausfather, who is watching the situation unfold. “It’s not a great story.”.

Sources indicate that el Niño is one phase of a natural climate pattern called the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, which has a dramatic impact on global rainfall patterns. El Niño years are marked by unusually warm waters in the tropical Pacific, which weaken winds across that patch and alter global patterns of rising and falling air pressure. The results are complicated and variable, but they tend to bring dry conditions to some tropical areas—including the Amazon and parts of Australia and Africa—and rain to other places, including Florida. The other side of the oscillation, La Niña, is marked by cooler ocean temperatures and a different pattern of wet and dry. The planet swings between the two in irregular intervals of years, sometimes with neutral periods in between.

It has been revealed that both sides of this cycle can harm crops, though one prominent 2014 study found that El Niño affects a larger swath of the globe’s harvested land. While some places get more water, and some crops thrive, in many spots drought withers production. That same study found that an El Niño tends to improve global soybean production by up to 5 percent but suppresses maize, rice, and wheat by up to 4 percent. The numbers in any one country can be much more dramatic than that: Since 1980, South Africa’s maize output, for example, has averaged about 28 percent below normal during El Niño years.

Cereal disruptions, even if small, can hit hard if they come on top of other economic strains, states Stanford agricultural economist David Lobell. “When markets are tight, then if there’s a drought somewhere, that’s a much bigger deal.”.

Recent findings suggest that and the markets are, indeed, tight. Global average food prices have been trending upwards for about 20 years, says Lobell, thanks to climate blows stacking on top of each other. And this year has brought additional strains. When the U.S. and Israel launched an attack on Iran at the end of February, marine traffic through the Strait of Hormuz ground to a near halt for months. The transport of oil was choked, energy prices spiked, and the supply of fertilizer, which is most often made with hydrogen sourced from cheap natural gas, was severely pinched. The Middle East usually produces a quarter of the world’s fertilizer. Meanwhile, the ongoing war in Ukraine continues to play havoc with the cost of fuel and restrict the transport of wheat from a major hub on the Black Sea.

As of October, the warming in the mid-tropical Pacific that’s used to measure the strength of an El Niño hit 3.5 degrees Celsius—breaking the previous record of about 2.75 degrees Celsius—and is on its way to an unprecedented peak of around 4 degrees, according to Hausfather. “That’s scary,” he states. Broadly speaking, he says, the more powerful the El Niño, the more powerful its effects on weather events, including droughts.

Recent findings suggest that unusually, this year’s El Niño is the third “strong” El Niño event to hit within a relatively short span of 11 years, which means some areas have been hit repeatedly with drought. The higher-than-usual frequency of El Niños may itself be caused by climate change, some researchers have suggested—though this is still an area of hot debate, Hausfather says.

In a recent development, all these factors act together, with cascading impacts that can take months to develop and last for years. “The confluence of drought and conflict drives some of the worst outcomes we see,” claims Richard Choularton, director of climate and resilience for the World Food Programme in Rome. A farmer can’t afford fertilizer; then his fields face drought. In anticipation of a bad year, he plants less and hires fewer people. The river used to transport his crop dries up, and the port that takes it overseas has been bombed out of commission. His cows have little to eat. A year later, he can’t afford to buy groceries or fuel his farming equipment. The lack of rain allows seawater to seep into aquifers, so fresh water gets rationed. Hydropower plants sputter. And on it goes.

Industry observers note that while any year brings its own spates of bad weather—some of it random, and some made more likely by the pressures of climate change—plenty of events this year have been attributed to El Niño. Among the first to be hit was the Peruvian anchovy fishery, which was closed dramatically early this year to give anchovies a fighting chance in the face of warm waters and less plankton, one of their main food sources. This industry, typically worth between $2 billion and $3 billion, is a huge contributor to global feed for livestock and aquaculture. As of September, global fishmeal output was about half what it was the year before; fishmeal prices have spiked, with some European salmon farmers turning to cheaper chicken byproducts.

In Indonesia, palm oil mills stopped buying fruit from farmers because an ongoing drought shriveled the area’s main transportation artery, the Kapuas River. In Cambodia, a delayed rainy season is drying out rice fields. Panama has declared a national state of emergency (as it did for the 2023 and 2015 El Niños), and the Panama Canal is carrying less ship traffic and transporting less food in the face of dwindling rainfall. In northern Sudan, rainfall totals have been less than half of normal, which is expected to take a toll on both crops and livestock from March to August next year. El Niño-induced drought alongside record summer temperatures in Central America has eaten away at crop yields and threatens that region’s second planting cycle: The E.U.’s Joint Research Centre projects an 83 percent spike in people suffering from acute food insecurity in that area.

Perhaps surprisingly, the global food production outlook for this growing season isn’t as bad as one might think: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) notes that the USDA projects worldwide production of maize, wheat, and rice for 2026-2027 to be just 2.7 percent below the previous year’s production, which will still make it the second-largest annual crop on record.

“Globally, food supply is not of high concern,” says FEWS NET advisor Amy Ostrander. “The concerns are production changes in some specific regions, such as Southern Africa, and food access.” Even if sufficient crops are harvested in those regions, in other words, some food won’t make it to market, and some people won’t be able to afford it.

An analysis by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization concludes that the highest risks from El Niño–prompted droughts will be in the Sahel, Southern Africa, South and Southeast Asia, and in Central America’s Dry Corridor and the Caribbean.

One good thing about an El Niño is that meteorologists can see it coming almost a year in advance, unlike freak weather events, which are harder to forecast. This gives agencies a fighting chance to protect people by distributing drought-resistant seeds, for example, securing deals for future emergency food supplies and transport, or setting up income assistance for struggling farmers.

The World Food Programme first tested its forecast-based financing program in Zimbabwe during the 2015 El Niño: Delivering cash to families in one district facing drought helped them to sustain their quantity and quality of food, while a neighboring district that didn’t receive cash aid saw a massive drop. This year, the WFP has been delivering cash and other assistance, including, for example, more than 3,000 airtight silos for farmers in Guatemala to help them safely store grain. As of October, the program indicates it has reached 28 million people across 15 countries with early warning information and assistance.

In a recent development, cash is strapped for such programs, though. Funds for global aid were down 30 percent in 2025 from their 2022 peak and are still falling, making it hard for the WFP and others to do their work. In Somalia, the WFP helped 10 million people during a drought in 2022; today, in the face of similar conditions, indicates Choularton, they can afford to reach fewer than a million.

Sources indicate that advanced warning is good, notes Lobell, but challenges will still abound, and even harder times may lie ahead as El Niños pile on top of climate change. The peaks of strong El Niños are almost always followed by record-breaking years for the global average temperature. The anomalously hot years of 1998, 2016, and 2024 (the current record holder) all followed hot on the heels of El Niño peaks the year before. While 2026 is warm, “2027 is going to be the record-shattering year,” says Hausfather.

Global warming, of course, also has impacts on food supply. Last year, Lobell published a paper showing that total wheat, barley, maize, rice, and soybean yields are now altogether about 5 percent lower overall than they would have been in a world without climate change. “To a lot of people, that sounds like a small number. But the kind of shocks that we talk about can be far smaller than that,” he says. “It doesn’t take much of a supply shift to have an vital effect on people’s lives.”.

Because the specific places that get warmer and drier during El Niños are different from the specific places that get warmer and drier from climate change, researchers caution that what we see in 2026 won’t be a precise forerunner of things to come. But how we deal with this temporary challenge does say something about the resilience of our food systems, states Lobell, and it will reveal how we might cope in the future with other climate disruptions to crops. “That’s one of the big questions,” he says. “How much can you adapt when the conditions are bad?”.

COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
  • After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU noted it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.
  • Industry observers note that "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU noted it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

Industry observers note that "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," noted Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required.".

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

"Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation noted.

The Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠noted the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

In a recent development, pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," said the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing. Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

The final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs.".

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, stated TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed prepares for a global transformation.".

It has been revealed that at the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

In a recent development, it included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

According to recent reports, the talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot.".

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”.

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Another contenious problem at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text noted the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu mentioned carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve.".

Industry observers note that the stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, mentioned his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

According to recent reports, "We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation.".

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.
  • Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.

Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.

It has been revealed that created by German developer Gregor Weichbrodt with music by Scott Hühnerkrisp, a new sandwich simulator is exactly that. "You make a sandwich. That's all," reads the simulator's about page. Notably, it's not the same as FiftyEight Studios' 2026 game Sandwich Simulator or Sandwich Squad's 2024 Sandwich Sim.

According to recent reports, each sandwich gets a serial number and a permalink, so you can revisit your creation later for reasons I can't quite conjure here beyond lunch inspo. To date, 42,375 unique sandwiches have been made on the simulator since it released in Oct. 2026. For example, my tower of power sandwich will probably live on the internet after I shuffle off this mortal coil.

But there's more going on here, with the developer promising "realistic cucumber behavior" (if you put a slice too far on the edge it'll fall off) and "soft body physics" (slices of cheese, salmon, or ham will drape themselves over what's already on the sandwich).

To make a sandwich, all you need to do is add toppings from the array provided in the bottom menu. To add spreads, you tap the pot and a virtual knife will appear; holding your mouse down will drag that butter across the bread. For other toppings like cheese, radishes, crisps, eggs, tomatoes, and whatnot, you just drag your pick from the menu onto your bread.

If you want to get rid of anything, because you've realised you hate radish (you monster), you can just drag it onto the board. And once you're happy with your creation, you can tap the photo button to save it and generate your permalink — a page which gives you a delightful description of all the ingredients. You can also see every sandwich that has ever been created on the game.

Yes, this might be the era of GTA 6, but between missions I'll be making salad sandwiches and drawing my own aquarium. Bit of balance, right?

#139023. Latest Update: What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1149 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1149 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK.
  • Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery?
  • But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

According to recent reports, the Spanish city of Barcelona recently declared that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

In a recent development, how did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”.

According to recent reports, after all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. Upcoming York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

Industry observers note that this dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

In a recent development, this elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an vital relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today indicates this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered key friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”.

According to recent reports, society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”.

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s newly introduced cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of Newly introduced York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

Industry observers note that the RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the latest Barcelona cemetery, it is notable to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

Join us on Twitter and Facebook.

Sources indicate that this will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the crucial animals in your life.

#139021. Breaking: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1719 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • Industry observers note that for 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt.
  • Sources indicate that they waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

Industry observers note that for 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

Sources indicate that they waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil demonstrated no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

Fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

In a recent development, now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine mentioned.

The experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” said Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”.

According to recent reports, when he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined promptly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

When he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

It has been revealed that convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

They considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

Sources indicate that through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining demonstrated no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

Industry observers note that for six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples indicated higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

During metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

In a recent development, he devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

For Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

According to recent reports, the idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran stated.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, stated Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

“This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he said of the new work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

Another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, noted Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

According to recent reports, ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he said. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

However, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet said. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet mentioned, “right there under our feet.”.

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart noted global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

According to recent reports, walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the company has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner said in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

Recent findings suggest that CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

Industry observers note that "This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

According to recent reports, walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

According to recent reports, walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the manufacturer performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, the firm reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Sources indicate that walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Recent findings suggest that furner also said Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he stated.

Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

In October, Walmart confirmed it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

Furner told CNBC the new membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the tech giant reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The firm on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

Sources indicate that the firm is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company stated it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey said Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

The significant-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.
  • In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law.
  • After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”.

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put upcoming restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the problem of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

Sources indicate that that’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, remarked that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about aims to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

In a recent development, the CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

In a recent development, so is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the problems that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

In a recent development, they’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

It sounds like CEOs are frustrated?

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

It has been revealed that you would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from massive business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Recent findings suggest that tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

Industry observers note that the first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two upcoming factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

Industry observers note that “Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Nations reported on Sunday a drone attack on a residential area in Khartoum, Sudan's capital.

A UN building located in a civilian neighborhood was damaged in the attack, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

"It is unacceptable that we are put at such risk," noted the UN's Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown.

The AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around Khartoum Airport and in other parts of the city from approximately 2:00 a.m. to 4:30 a.m. local time.

In a recent development, according to a witness, a drone strike completely destroyed a house. There were no immediate reports of casualties.

Meanwhile, a Sudanese army source noted the drones had been launched from Ethiopia.

Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of allowing attacks to be launched from its territory. However, Addis Ababa has denied these accusations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Sudan has been engulfed in a civil war since April 2023. The army of de facto ruler Abdel-Fattah al-Burhan and the RSF militia led by Mohamed Hamdan Daglo have been fighting for control of the country.

The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced more than 14 million.

According to UN data, the use of drones has dramatically altered the course of the war this year, killing more than 1,100 people in the first six months.

The UN also stated that of the hundreds of child casualties this year, two-thirds were killed or injured by drone strikes.

Just days ago, a Sudanese army drone strike killed 15 people, including four children, in a West Kordofan village. The army was advancing through the state and recapturing territory from the RSF.

#139012. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (936 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday.
  • Sources indicate that AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026.
  • Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s new terms.

Sources indicate that AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power people latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

In a recent development, some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

According to recent reports, it’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently confirmed that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

In a recent development, the automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get people in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Recent findings suggest that banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major concerns, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data demonstrates that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” indicates Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

It has been revealed that “The banks see risks with everything,” she states. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”.

Sources indicate that even though outliers exist, many people are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

He sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, big-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

In a recent development, cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express announced that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

Banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” People have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its latest EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even launched an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

Recent findings suggest that despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The issue with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she says. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.
