Gap names fresh Athleta CEO, states Old Navy turnaround is seeing signs of progress

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec.
  • The retailer also mentioned Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.
  • Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.

The retailer also mentioned Old Navy's turnaround is showing signs of progress, sending shares up more than 11% Friday.

Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.

Sources indicate that "I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter stated in a statement.

The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.

According to recent reports, "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode.".

Recent findings suggest that dickson stated the tech giant is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.

While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson mentioned this latest approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.

It has been revealed that gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.

Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the tech giant said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.

Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.

The manufacturer lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.

Dickson stated in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.

"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

It has been revealed that for the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.

At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. `.

Recent findings suggest that the firm's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson remarked it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.

"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson stated.

The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its newly introduced CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.

Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the manufacturer attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.

Dickson mentioned the brand has since introduced fresh products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.

"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth.".

#139003. Tech Report: Best Gifts for Mom (2026): Digital Wall Calendars, Better Bags, Personalized Jewelry, and More

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Best Gifts for Mom (2026): Digital Wall Calendars, Better Bags, Personalized Jewelry, and More

📅 05 May 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love.
  • Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that moms give the best gifts, so it stands to reason that you should get the best gifts for Mom when you're shopping for her in any scenario. That includes Mother's Day, her birthday, Christmas, Hanukkah, or any other holiday in your family's life that includes gift-giving. The holiday season is now upon us, and I've added a few gift ideas with that time of year in mind.

Recent findings suggest that if you're worried you're going to give her a disappointing gift or something she already has, fear not: I've gathered the coolest things we recommend here at WIRED that just about any mom will love. From wellness gadgets that can improve her skin to the best tote bags I've tried, and even a device that puts her digital calendar in an IRL device, moms everywhere can get a ton out of these gifts. Many of these are items I've given to my mother, or other WIRED staffers have given to theirs. Or they might be at the top of my own wish list as a mother of a 4-year-old.

Updated November 2026: I've added Therabody's Theraface Mask Glo, Omnilux's Contour Gloves, WanderFull's HydroBag, and Nuuly's clothing subscription as new gifts to this guide.

The must-have gadget for women of almost any age is an LED mask. These masks promise to use red light to erase wrinkles, brighten your skin, and keep acne at bay. I haven't seen much change in my wrinkles in my year-plus of regularly using a red-light mask, but I can confirm it makes my skin brighter and calms down acne and scars much faster when I'm regularly treating my skin, and I always get compliments on how nice my skin looks when I'm regularly using it. Therabody's TheraFace Mask Glo has a range of treatments with both red and blue light, a unique vibration therapy feature, and removable eye shields if you don't want the light in your eyes.

Recent findings suggest that look, nothing says mom life like looking for the perfect bag. I'm in a massive tote phase of my life; I somehow need to either lug an armload of items for myself and my son (or just myself!) or I only need a tiny belt bag. There's no in between.

In a recent development, the Yardsale Day Bag has been my go-to for a variety of needs, from a colorful personal item for a flight to a gym bag to the aerial studio. It's got a waterproof bottom that makes me happy to bring it to the zoo's splash pad, and a magnetic middle separator you can flex to separate the middle of the bag into two medium sections to better divide all your items. Plus, there are a handful of side pockets inside, but none are large enough for my massive Owala water bottle. I have the 30L in Butter, but there's also a smaller 20L version if you're looking for something a little more compact.

It has been revealed that if your mom wants something a little more stylish, the Alex Mill totes are always on my mind. They come in a variety of gorgeous colors and are made of coated canvas, so they can put up with daily adventures, and you can customize them with your mom's initials (or even just the word “mom”!) with Alex Mill's hand-painted letter service. It's a simpler tote with no other pockets, but you can use the top snaps to let out the sides or tuck them in, depending on how much space Mom needs on a given day. The weathered color and vibe of these bags also feel perfect for the fall season.

In a recent development, my latest favorite family planning gadget is a digital wall calendar. These handy devices take the Google Calendar I live by (and just about any other digital calendar, if your mom isn't a Google girl) and put it on a physical device I can promptly tap into without needing to grab my phone or bark at Alexa. The Skylight Calendar 2 is my favorite, because it not only includes to-do lists, meal planning, and a recipe book but also doubles as a digital photo frame. That means it displays cute photos of my family most of the time, and then, with a simple tap, it opens the calendar or whatever page I was last on to show me what's on my family's schedule. It does have a subscription fee, though, to get the digital photo frame feature and a few other options, like meal planning. But I think it's well worth it to get so many features in a single device. You can also gift her kiddo a Skylight Buddy ($140) so that she doesn't have to remind them to check the main calendar for their chores; it'll appear on their own device if they have a Buddy.

Recent findings suggest that to me, motherhood is all about change. It's most obvious at the start of motherhood, when your body changes a lot over the course of nine months, but motherhood encompasses the rest of our lives, and our bodies and style change a lot over that time. One of the biggest giveaways that time has gone by is our clothes—how well they fit for our current stage, whether they reflect the time of our life right now, and if we're bored out of our skull with everything but don't want to buy an entirely latest closet.

I've been loving renting from Nuuly this pregnancy because the brand has an entire maternity section that lets me find pieces to fit me in this short—but very different size—season of my life. My older mother also loves having a clothing subscription because she gets bored of her outfit options to wear into the office, and I loved it for the same reason when I had my first clothing subscription right out of college. If Mom has been talking about wanting some fresh looks but feels overwhelmed about what she wants to invest in, these rental services are a fun way to get a lot of new clothes in your life without having to store them or spend as much as you would have (some of my favorite maternity clothes I've gotten through Nuuly would have cost me $200 apiece!) The service costs $98 a month, but your first month is discounted to just $60. There's one piece I miss already that might drive me to pick up a second subscription, which would genuinely be cheaper than buying the piece I want brand new.

It has been revealed that for years, the go-to gift for a woman in my family, mother or not, was shopping in the jewelry section of a department store. My mom even helped orchestrate this for the rest of the aunties and grandmas, but now, as a mom myself, I find myself interested in jewelry that tells a story about my family and children instead of just any old set. (Except extra earrings for my earring stack, a gift I'm thrilled to get, because there's never enough.).

I love these pieces from Gorjana and BaubleBar that you can customize. Gorjana has a ton of charms you can add to its necklaces or bracelets to reflect Mom’s kids’ initials, birthstones, or anything else; I paired a charm of my son’s first initial ($50) with the Wilshire Adjustable Necklace ($68). If she's more of a ring gal, BaubleBar's Toi et Moi ring ($78) lets you choose two birthstones to display. I chose my and my son's birthstones, but luckily his sibling-to-be will also have a red birthstone, so it'll remain a perfect reflection of my kids and me for years to come.

This item was literally made for sports moms: a padded stadium cushion with a wearable blanket inside. My son plays on three sports teams, so I do a lot of sitting outside on bleachers and turf sidelines—and often at night, when it’s freezing. I’ve tried many things to keep warm, from heated jackets to HotHands, but nothing has worked as well as this water-resistant blanket, which unfurls to 50 x 70 inches and sports a clip at the front so you can wear it like a cape. It can also be used for picnics or as a spot for younger siblings to sit and read during tournaments. It’s also not hard to fold it back up and fit it inside the seat part (which is 1 inch thick without the blanket inside). It comes in six colors, so you can be sure to find one that matches your giftee’s kid’s team or school colors. —Kat Merck.

As a mom, I take a lot of photos of my family. A lot. And sometimes it feels like all those great photos of my son's milestones go to my camera roll and photo storage to die. There are two solutions I love for this that are incredibly giftable: a digital photo frame she can instantly upload images to, and a printed photo book where you can take the best of the best and put them at her fingertips. I have and love both for different reasons.

I love the digital photo frame to add all the photos from a fun weekend at the San Diego Zoo or Renaissance Pleasure Faire for me to relive again and again, but I also love being able to pull a photo book from the bookshelf and relive a specific moment I know is waiting there for me. Aura makes my favorite digital photo frames (followed by Skylight's Calendar 2 if you want a multipurpose device, but Aura has no subscription fee if you only want photos), while Mixbook has been a favorite of mine for a while when it comes to printing photos, and has great starting prices for its photo books.

The graduation from diaper-bag-carrying mom to tote-full-of-snacks-and-clothes-changes mom to an adult who only needs to carry their own stuff is a parenting milestone that deserves celebration. This is my favorite grown-up mom bag, which holds only the essentials: water (because no matter how old your kids are, someone is going to get thirsty), cards, phone, and keys. The thick strap makes it comfortable to carry, and there’s a color, material, or theme for just about anyone’s vibe, including a new line of clear stadium versions. All WanderFull bags will hold any handle-less water bottle up to 11 inches tall and 3.5 inches in diameter. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that once my kiddo is asleep, you can find me parked on the couch playing video games. I upgraded to a Nintendo Switch 2 ($499) earlier this summer so I could finally buy and play Pokopia ($70), since it's exclusive to the upcoming console, and now my husband and I are completely hooked on the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time ($60) remake that came out a few weeks ago. It's also rapidly become an experience I can share with my son now that he's 4; he was been helping me and my husband replay Tears of the Kingdom, but now he's dubbed Ocarina of Time as “Big Little Link” and is obsessed with using the grappling hook and using up all of our arrows.

If you're not looking to upgrade her console just yet but need a Switch-friendly cozy game for her, Stardew Valley has another massive update in the works and only costs $15. I'm also hoping we see Fields of Mistria ($14) come to the Switch eventually, but the full launch came out in August for Steam people and has major quality-of-life improvements if she has played Stardew one time too many. My husband also upgraded his gaming setup this summer with a Steam Machine (from $1,049), and I have big aims to start using it often for Fields of Mistria. If your mom loves games, she'll love any one of these new devices or new games, especially if she already got herself the new gadget as I did.

If a mom in your life is exploring her nonalcoholic drink options, The Zero Proof has some gift sets perfect to give so she can try out several things at once. I'm currently grounded from drinking any cocktails while I'm pregnant, but moms (and people in general) can have all kinds of reasons to want to explore unique, interesting drinks that are sans alcohol. I really liked this set for how many cool drinks it exposed me to, from bottles of nonalcoholic wine to knockoff cocktails. If you're looking to spend a little less, my favorites so far have been the Château del Ish Non-Alcoholic Sparkling Espumante ($20) and Lapo's Non-Alcoholic Melograno Mule ($20 for four).

Look, I love a Kindle, but if you want to get the best e-reader for your buck (or maybe she just wants an e-reader that isn't a Kindle), the answer is actually a Kobo. My favorite is the Kobo Libra Colour. It's cheaper than the Kindle Colorsoft and can also double as a digital notebook if you add on the $70 stylus. I also prefer Kobo's annotating options: You can write right on the pages instead of in weird pop-up margins and boxes only on Kindle. Kobo also has a page-turner remote ($34), which I love to pair with a pillow stand holder so I can lean back and relax without holding up my e-reader while I read. I gave a similar pillow stand to my mom, and now I can spot her last reading spot easily because that pillow is resting there.

You could also gift her one of the upcoming Kindles if she's a Kindle addict. Many of my friends are drooling over the new purple Ube color of the 12th-gen Kindle ($150), but my personal favorite is the Kindle Aluminum (I just wish it were cheaper!). There's also finally Kindle page-turn remote, the Kindle Click ($35).

In a recent development, if the mom you know is into LED red-light therapy, she probably already knows about face masks and hair growth devices like the one we recommend above, but there’s one area she’s probably neglecting: her hands. With aging comes loss of collagen, subcutaneous fat, and cumulative effects of UV exposure. I spent the first 26 years of my life living in California, where I rarely remembered to put sunscreen on the tops of my hands. Twenty years later, it reveals—they’re wrinkly and have age spots and look like they belong to someone 15 years my senior. Trust me; no mom wants this. I’ve been using Omnilux’s FDA-cleared red-light glove for the past few months to try to mitigate some of the damage, and while I haven’t seen any changes yet (Omnilux says changes happen in four to six weeks, but in my experience with red-light masks, it typically takes much longer to see results), I very much enjoy using this device on its own. The soft silicone glove is comfortable to wear and warms as it heats up, so it feels good and works to reduce joint pain. It’s easy to do while I’m reading or watching TV—just three 10-minute sessions per week—and the rechargeable battery (USB-C) lasts a little over a week. If your giftee already spends 10 minutes at the end of the day relaxing in an LED face mask, she’ll know exactly what to do here. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that if you know a mom who loves to bird-watch (I know one!), you can upgrade her bird feeder to a smart one. Smart bird feeders add a camera to the feeder so she can see a close-up feed of the birds that come to hang out in her yard, and they're adorable to boot, for a little smart curb appeal. WIRED reviewer Kat Merck recommends the original Birdfy feeder as a great gift; it's her favorite smart bird feeder and comes in adorable colors to brighten your mom's yard and catch the eye of neighborhood birds. But the one she and I both have our eye on (her for her mother, me for myself) is the Birdfy Nest Duo, which is actually a birdhouse with two cameras so you can see the birds entering the nest outside and raising a family inside.

It has been revealed that I love a backpack when I'm on the move with my 4-year-old, but one thing that annoys me is that things are hard to find inside, because packs are typically so deep. That's why I adore the Mina Baie Emmy Diaper Bag: It's a wide, shallow bag instead of a long one, making it easy to open and see most of what I store in it without digging around. I'm not toting diapers at the moment, but I've used it to pack a ton of snacks, toys, and spare clothing for my kid.

Recent findings suggest that I'm intrigued to see how using it with two kids goes—I chose the Emmy Midi, which is the midsize bag, but if you're a pumping parent or need to carry a ton of bottles with formula, you might want to try the larger Emmy Full. The stylish bag is made of vegan leather and can be converted from crossbody to tote to backpack mode, depending on which straps you use. Mina Baie doesn't include a changing kit, but sells one separately ($59) if you'd like to include it in your gift (or buy that as the gift to upgrade their existing bag of choice).

Industry observers note that if Mom loves entertaining—or just being festive—but doesn’t want to have to store a million different dishes, Nora Fleming’s modular serving-tray system is for her. First, pick a base—there are trays, baking dishes, utensil crocks, and even salt and pepper shakers. Then, pick one of dozens of hand-painted “Minis,” or ceramic accents (sold separately). There are holiday themes, sports team themes, and even ones for specific events like mah-jongg or BBQs.

Each base has a hole into which you can attach the Mini with a little rubber stopper. I tested the cracker tray with a harvest-themed Mini, and you wouldn’t know the tray didn’t come with the accent already attached. At the end of next month, I plan to swap it out for a Christmas tree Mini, and so on. Best part is that if Mom likes this setup, you’ll be set on gifts for the foreseeable future, provided you can keep finding new Minis you think she’ll like. —Kat Merck.

Industry observers note that I'm expecting again, and this time I'm on a mission to find a good pregnancy pillow. I tried a large body pillow on the advice of another site for my first pregnancy, and it was honestly an awful experience—the pillow was too large and firm for me to comfortably use, let alone have room for both it and my growing midsection in my bed. Plus, it was heavy, which is annoying when your body already feels too cumbersome to move around.

So far, using the Wildbird Pregnancy Pillow has been the opposite. It's slim and light with just enough squish to add a little support under or around my belly without being difficult to get comfortable. It’s beautiful and easy to maneuver around. Wildbird also suggests it for other support positions postpartum, and I'm curious if those will work for me. But it makes for a beautiful gift for any expecting mom and will be one she's excited to put on her bed and curl up with at night.

Recent findings suggest that for most moms, showers are sacred—especially for moms of babies or younger kids. However, heavy metals, sediments, chlorine, and PFAS can cause health problems not just in drinking water but in water that touches the skin, as well. They can also cause buildup on hair and shower surfaces, making them harder to clean. Many municipalities—including mine—treat water with chlorine, and when I asked him which filter he'd recommend for my own shower, former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage suggested the Weddell Duo. It's the only US filter he's found that has certification for chlorine and lead removal from NSF International, and it also cites third-party testing by IAPMO R&T showing it can remove PFAS, though there's no corresponding certification.

Still, the Duo has a 2.5-gallon-per-minute flow rate and can remove most chlorine from over 8,000 gallons' worth of showers. It's an in-line filter, so it's easy to install in minutes—just screw it in between your pipe and showerhead. It even comes with a little roll of waterproof tape to ensure a leak-free fit, and because of the horizontal orientation, installation won't affect the showerhead height. The filter needs to be replaced every three months, but refills only run about $25 each, compared with competitors like Filterbaby or Rorra, which can cost $40 to $45. —Kat Merck.

Tech Report: HSBC's top execs face tense shareholders calling for a breakup

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.
  • At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.
  • In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

HSBC’s top brass defended their strategy Monday to frustrated shareholders in the lender’s largest market, as Europe’s biggest bank continued to face calls to be split up.

At an informal shareholder meeting in Hong Kong, Chairman Mark Tucker and CEO Noel Quinn took questions from investors on issues ranging from how the bank was approaching demands for an overhaul of its business to its purchase of Silicon Valley Bank’s UK arm.

In prepared remarks, Tucker and Quinn each reiterated the board’s recommendation that shareholders vote against a resolution on the docket for its annual general meeting in May that would force the bank to come up with a plan to spin off or reorganize its Asian business — the lender’s main source of profits.

HSBC's biggest shareholder reignites debate about breaking up the bank.

Tucker said the board was unanimous in its opposition to the resolution, stating plainly: “It would not be in your interest to split the bank.”.

He remarked the board had previously reviewed a range of options for restructuring the bank, and concluded that such alternatives would “materially destroy value for shareholders,” including dividends.

Sources indicate that “Our strategy is working,” Tucker told the room of more than 1,000 shareholders. “Our current strategy is moving dividends up.”.

HSBC has been facing calls to separate its Asian business from the rest of the bank over the past year.

Shareholders in Hong Kong — where HSBC is a mainstay of many retail investors’ portfolios — contend that the London-based lender’s performance has been dragged down by its businesses in other regions.

Quinn addressed those complaints head-on Monday, saying “our profits in Hong Kong and the UK are no longer being dragged down by underperformance elsewhere. The group is performing well as a whole.”.

Pressed later by a shareholder on the glitch, Quinn said a breakup of the bank would result in “significant revenue loss” because much of its business relied on cross-border transactions.

In a recent development, investors have also been unhappy with HSBC scrapping its dividend in 2020, at the request of British regulators. They argue that if the lender cordoned off its activities in Asia, it would no longer have to expose Hong Kong shareholders to requests in other jurisdictions.

Christine Fong, a district council member in Hong Kong, noted she represented about 500 small shareholders who had been affected by the dividend cancellation.

“Street hawkers, taxi drivers or teachers — they all relied on the dividend to pay for their regular expenses, like mortgage, insurance payments, school fees,” Fong told CNN.

“That’s why, three years ago, what HSBC did upset those small minority shareholders.”.

Fong has now joined calls for shareholders to vote in favor of the proposal for the bank to spin off its Asian business, despite the lender bringing back its dividend in 2021, albeit at a lower level.

Ken Lui, an activist shareholder in Hong Kong who put the resolution together, doubled down on his call for support ahead of the meeting Monday.

The resolution will require 75% of votes to be passed in May, but “nothing is impossible,” he told reporters outside the meeting venue.

Lui, who said he personally held a stake worth 100 million Hong Kong dollars ($12.7 million), laid out plans for his team to focus on “targeted outreach to institutional shareholders to present our case and gain their support.”.

His group will also canvass 18 districts of Hong Kong “to tell HSBC shareholders that they finally have a chance to speak for themselves and protect their rights through voting,” he added.

HSBC is also facing pressure from its largest shareholder.

Ping An (PNGAY), China’s biggest insurer, holds an 8% stake in HSBC and has backed calls for the bank to rethink its structure.

In a series of remarks made public by the Chinese firm last November, Huang Yong, chairman of Ping An’s asset management arm, noted “we will support any initiatives including a spinoff that are conducive to improve HSBC’s performance and value.”.

Since then, the insurance giant’s views haven’t changed, according to a person familiar with the matter.

The source told CNN that Ping An has been calling for HSBC to explore a reorganization, with an eye on boosting its valuation and simplifying its regulatory obligations around the globe.

The insurer has not recommended a specific path forward but will support any initiatives, including a spinoff of its Asian business, that could boost its stock performance or value, the person added. Ping An did not immediately respond to a request for comment on how it planned to vote at the upcoming general meeting.

Industry observers note that HSBC’s leaders were also asked Monfday why the bank had scooped up the British unit of SVB following the stunning collapse of its parent in the United States. The purchase was made for £1 ($1.20) last month, just days after SVB had folded.

Critics have questioned HSBC’s ability to perform adequate due diligence on SVB UK’s customers because of how rapidly the deal came together.

It has been revealed that “Did HSBC look into the clients of SVB in detail? Say, the financial statement — whether they can pay back the loan?” said Fong.

HSBC buys SVB's UK business, ending 'nightmare' for British tech.

Recent findings suggest that quinn and Tucker defended the acquisition, calling it a good business opportunity that allowed the bank to gain hundreds of innovative startups as customers. They pushed back on the notion that management hadn’t had time to carry out proper due diligence.

Tucker also weighed in on recent tumult in the banking industry, saying he did not expect an “immediate impact” on HSBC.

“After the collapse of a number of smaller regional banks and the takeover of Credit Suisse, the share prices of all banks have been suppressed,” he noted.

According to recent reports, but he said he did not believe such developments represented “a systemic risk” to the sector. “I do expect a period of uncertainty” before nerves settle, he added.

Turkey: Thousands protest closure of critical media outlets

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey.
  • Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.
  • They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several thousand people in Istanbul took to the streets on Sunday to protest the closure of several opposition-linked media outlets in Turkey.

Protesters chanted, cheered, and whistled as they marched several kilometers through the city, calling for press freedom and freedom of expression.

They carried a huge banner that read: "We want freedom of thought, freedom of the press, and freedom for journalists." The protesters were also carrying placards that read, "The press cannot be silenced.".

Turkey's main opposition party, Yeni Parti, called for a protest just days after police raided Sozcu TV, one of the last opposition-aligned television channels.

Senior staff members were arrested during the raid. A government-appointed trustee was installed, and the TV manufacturer was placed under compulsory administration.

It was the third takeover in a year following similar actions against Tele1, Halk TV, Turkey's most-watched news channel, and the leading digital news website, T24.

Timur Soykan, a journalist who was briefly detained for criticizing the government, stated that the government was doing everything in its power to silence journalists but was failing to do so.

Soykan asked the public to support Halk TV journalists, who plan to continue broadcasting on a upcoming YouTube channel.

Over the past decade, press freedom has faced sustained pressure in the form of prosecutions, digital censorship, and government accusations that journalists are spreading "fake news.".

It has been revealed that in the last two months alone, Turkey has arrested several journalists for their reporting on a multibillion-dollar investment fund scandal. At least two of the journalists remain in pretrial detention.

According to the media rights group MLSA, twenty-five journalists are currently imprisoned in Turkey.

This year, Reporters Without Borders ranked Turkey 163rd out of 180 countries in its Press Freedom Index.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China Renaissance, a top dealmaker in the country’s tech industry, said it would suspend trading of its shares and delay the release of its annual results because it still can’t get in touch with its founder.

Bao Fan, 52, started the boutique investment bank in 2005 and has been unreachable since the middle of February, according to the company. Shares in China Renaissance have plunged since Bao went missing, at one point dropping as much as 50%.

Industry observers note that china Renaissance said in late February that it had learned Bao was “cooperating in an investigation” being carried out by certain authorities in the country. It gave no other details.

Chinese media have reported Bao might be assisting in an investigation related to a former executive at China Renaissance.

Recent findings suggest that in a filing on Sunday, China Renaissance remarked auditors couldn’t complete their work or sign off on their report because of Bao’s absence. The board was also unable to give an estimate about when it would be able to approve its audited results for 2022 or dispatch its annual report by an April 30 deadline as required by Hong Kong’s listing rules.

Missing Chinese billionaire CEO assisting authorities in investigation, company claims.

Trading in the company’s shares was suspended from Monday as a result.

Bao is known as a veteran dealmaker who works closely with top technology companies in China. He helped broker the 2015 merger between two of the country’s leading food delivery services, Meituan and Dianping. Today, the combined manufacturer’s “super app” platform is ubiquitous in China.

His team has also invested in US-listed Chinese electric vehicle makers Nio (NIO) and Li Auto and helped Chinese internet giants Baidu (BIDU) and JD.com (JD) complete their secondary listings in Hong Kong.

Sources indicate that over the weekend, China’s top anti-graft watchdog launched an investigation into Liu Liange, former party secretary and chairman of Bank of China, according to a statement by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection and the State Supervision Commission. The bank is state-owned and one of the country’s four biggest lenders.

Industry observers note that liu is suspected of “serious violations of discipline and law,” the statement remarked. He is among the most senior financial executives targeted in a broader financial crackdown by President Xi Jinping.

In January, Wang Bin, former party chief and chairman of China Life Insurance, was charged by national-level prosecutors with taking bribes and hiding overseas savings.

— Michelle Toh contributed reporting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.
  • A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.
  • The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Independent movie studio A24 has had a banner year at the box office, and HBO Max is set up to benefit from its success.

A24 is behind some of this year's buzziest films, including horror hit "Backrooms," dark comedy "The Drama" starring Zendaya and Robert Pattinson, and the Elizabeth Holmes documentary "You Can See Everything," co-directed by Nathan Fielder.

The studio has generated more than $526 million at the domestic box office this year as of Nov. 15, according to data from Rentrak. That's already roughly $290 million, or more than 50%, above its haul for all of 2025.

"They have an identity all their own, and just the mere mention of A24, the recognition that a movie is from A24, gives it instant credibility and provides a must-see factor, no matter what the subject matter," Paul Dergarabedian, head of marketplace trends at Rentrak, told CNBC.

Skydance co-CEO and Chairman David Ellison cited movie releases from A24 as part of the company's "unmatched portfolio" during its most recent earnings call.

A24 films released this year broke records at the box office, with "Backrooms" becoming the studio's biggest domestic opening to date and "You Can See Everything" notching the biggest documentary opening since "Fahrenheit 9/11" in 2004.

That success has already begun to translate to HBO Max's platform.

When "Backrooms" began streaming on HBO Max, it was the most streamed title on the platform for two weeks, according to Nielsen data. The film was also the fourth overall most streamed title the week it premiered, racking up 226 million minutes of viewing time.

After more than a year of competing bids and regulatory hurdles, Skydance now oversees two of the world's largest streaming platforms: HBO Max and Paramount+.

The company aims to eventually merge the streaming services into a single platform. It will take the first step in that effort by offering a value bundle in early 2027.

The combination of the platforms "will drive stronger engagement and higher lifetime value," co-CEO Ynon Kreiz noted on the company's earnings call earlier this month.

Paramount Skydance's direct-to-consumer segment, which includes Paramount+ and its free, ad-supported channel, Pluto TV, generated more than $2 billion in revenue during the third quarter, representing more than 35% of total revenue for the period. That segment revenue marked an 11% year-over-year increase, with revenue from Paramount+ up 21%.

The earnings do not reflect the Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition, since that deal closed after the close of the quarter.

Revenue growth in streaming will be important as it faces the daunting task of managing nearly $80 billion of debt.

The company has stated it expects to realize $6 billion in cost savings over the next three years and has put a particular focus on consolidating its operations and streamlining its marketing spend.

8 Best Travel Adapters (2026): 20+ Models Tested

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land.
  • The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.
  • Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

It has been revealed that there’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

For all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

In a recent development, perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

According to recent reports, when I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any complications with the UK prongs.

This budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

Recent findings suggest that what I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

Industry observers note that on the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

If you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a latest brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

Industry observers note that universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

This kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

Sources indicate that there is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

In a recent development, this cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

According to recent reports, it’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

Sources indicate that if you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Voltage converters are significant, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:.

Industry observers note that that should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

It has been revealed that if you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

Travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

According to recent reports, some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

Seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

Anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Industry observers note that epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that demonstrates you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

Statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

According to recent reports, satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

Industry observers note that baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Industry observers note that masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

Sources indicate that anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

Industry observers note that EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter.

In a recent development, ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

#138978. Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)

Rule-breaking is contagious — and good examples barely help

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty.
  • According to recent reports, A upcoming study suggests they become more likely to follow.
  • They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that most people stop at a red light, even when the road is empty. But what happens when the person next to them walks straight across?

According to recent reports, A upcoming study suggests they become more likely to follow. In an online experiment led by researchers at the University of Amsterdam, people who saw someone from their own political camp break a rule outright were nearly twice as likely to do the same. Seeing someone follow the rule barely made a difference.

A small number did more than copy. They broke the rule by more than the person they had watched. According to Lucas Molleman, an assistant professor of developmental psychology at the University of Amsterdam who led the research, a few bad actors like these can "basically take off the guardrails of the group.".

Sources indicate that the researchers wanted to know how seeing other people's choices affects whether someone sticks to a rule. They recruited 750 adults in the United States, roughly half Democrats and half Republicans, a week before the 2024 presidential election.

Participants watched an animated shooting star cross a row of 100 squares and were told to click the square where it shone brightest, which was always near the middle. Squares further to the right paid more money, so there was a reason to cheat.

Each person chose first on their own. They were then shown what a previous participant had done, whether that person had followed the rule, bent it or broken it outright, and which party they supported. Then they could change their answer. The task was repeated six times.

The experiment had no real-world stakes, and nobody was punished for cheating. Other researchers say that matters. "That's not how the world works," Eugen Dimant, a behavioral economist at the University of Pennsylvania who was not involved in the study, told Science News. Punishment and social pressure, he argues, also shape whether rule-breaking spreads.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that rule-breaking spread in the experiment. When people chose on their own, they picked the square furthest to the right, the most lucrative and most blatant violation, about 23% of the time. After seeing someone from their own party make that choice, they did so almost 40% of the time.

It has been revealed that small violations had only a small effect. Blatant ones had a much larger one.

It has been revealed that most people matched what they had seen or stayed below it. But just over 4% went further, breaking the rule by more than the person they had watched.

Good examples had little effect. Seeing a previous participant stick to the rule rarely changed what others did, even when that person was from their own party.

People also differed. Some followed the rule every time and others broke it every time, whatever they saw. The rest shifted depending on what others had done.

People were more likely to copy rule-breaking when it came from their own side. The effects were stronger when the person being watched shared the participant's political leanings.

Not everyone reads that as contagion. Stephen Reicher, a social psychologist at the University of St Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, told The Guardian that if influence depends on who the other person is, it does not spread the way a disease does. He pointed out that people who see a riot often turn up afterwards to help clean up.

According to recent reports, to see how individual choices might add up, the researchers ran computer simulations. They created a digital version of each participant and placed them in groups of 100.

In some scenarios, the handful of people prone to escalating pushed the whole group towards heavy rule-breaking. But when the simulated groups contained the same share of committed rule followers as the real experiment, rule-breaking leveled off at a moderate level.

It has been revealed that molleman calls the work fundamental science and claims the real world is far more complex. He sees possible links to situations such as drivers speeding together, or protests that turn violent.

In a recent development, he also claims it challenges how people see themselves. In individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, he said that people tend to believe they make their own decisions. But "in many, many cases we are very much influenced by what others are doing.".

This article is an excerpt from our podcast Science Unscripted.

#138971. Tech Report: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
  • Industry observers note that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.

Industry observers note that the makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.

Recent findings suggest that apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.

Sources indicate that it's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.

Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.

"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," remarked Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.

Recent findings suggest that fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves quickly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.

"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," stated U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20.".

But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.

The average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.

When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.

"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," said Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.

It has been revealed that though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.

Sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She noted that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.

It has been revealed that "There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman stated. "But I think both these trends are conflated.".

Sources indicate that nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.

Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.

It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.

Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, noted BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.

Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.

The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.

Recent findings suggest that "Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," said Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics.".

Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.

Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, remarked China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

"They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," stated Lu.

Industry observers note that alixPartners' Lapinsky remarked these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.

"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," noted BTIG's Stichter.

And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also said she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.

Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.

Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the manufacturer stated it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.

Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.

The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report. Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.

Alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.

Shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices. The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge.

Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the company is doing well.

"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," remarked AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027.".
