📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the barista at your neighborhood coffee shop knows your order before you even walk up to the counter, it might be time to consider learning to make that double Americano at home. With today being National Espresso Day and no shortage of espresso machines on sale ahead of Black Friday, that opportunity is particularly apt.

Industry observers note that each deal below is for a machine that a WIRED reviewer has tested and vetted in their own kitchen. If you take advantage of the savings now, your machine may arrive in time for Thanksgiving, allowing you to impress everyone with your post-dinner cappuccino-making skills.

For more deals, check out our Best Early Black Friday Deals, as well as early deals at Amazon and Home Depot.

Sources indicate that updated November 23: I’ve added upcoming deals on machines from Diletta, Fellow, and De'Longhi, plus some accessories. I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

WIRED reviewers have tried and liked a couple of machines from Diletta, a line of Italian-made, classic semiautomatics exclusive to Seattle Coffee Gear, and they’re all on sale today through December 14.

Sources indicate that we reviewed the Bello+ in 2024, appreciating the stylish, industrial design (handmade in Milan) and easily maneuverable steam wand. Our reviewer found it a bit finicky, but Seattle Coffee Gear says it does have a programmable pre-infusion for repeatable recipes.

According to recent reports, best Traditional Espresso Machine in our guide to the best, the Mio is stylish and built to last, with an analog design and a two-year warranty. It also makes for a solid first “real” espresso machine with its built-in shot timer and pressure gauge.

Recent findings suggest that fellow set some pretty lofty expectations with the release of its sleek Aiden coffee maker in 2024, and according to former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage, the brand didn't disappoint on its first attempt at an espresso machine. The ability to adjust flow rates and pressure curves was once the province of, as Korfhage put it, only the “richest and nerdiest of nerds.” But Fellow now allows you—yes, you, at home in your kitchen—to fine-tune how water moves through the grounds, unlocking previously unforeseen dimensions of flavor.

When we tested this machine, we liked it for a variety of reasons, including an easy-to-use milk frother and two swappable bean hoppers, which are especially helpful if you like to switch to decaf in the afternoons. It comes in a variety of finishes, but note that Beige is the cheapest of all right now, at only $915.

This flashy, design-oriented semiautomatic (“a steampunk gasworks of a thing,” according to Korfhage) is quite dramatic in person. It has a dual boiler—meaning you can froth milk at the same time you’re pulling a shot—and it comes with a nice set of accessories, including a tamper and milk pitcher. Note that this sale is on the 2nd Gen machine, which features expanded grinder settings and a newly introduced portafilter.

Formerly the Linea Classic, De’Longhi’s Classic is the best bare-bones espresso machine we’ve tried, with a pressure gauge, 15-bar pump, and updated thermoblock system. I used one for a full year and, while it’s not as foolproof as a semiautomatic, it was easy enough for morning espresso shots and cappuccinos; I even pulled off some rudimentary latte art with its steam wand.

Sources indicate that the Vertuo Pop+ is our favorite pod maker for espresso. The Deluxe model adds a larger, side-mount water tank (37 ounces to the original’s 25 ounces) and latest finishes, including this white one, a matte black-and-gold, and a sort of gunmetal gray.

It has been revealed that we appreciated this semiautomatic’s slim profile, consistent shots, and built-in burr grinder. The cold-brew setting is more of a gimmick than a way to make actual cold brew, and some design choices are a bit quirky. Even so, it’s a beautiful, industrial-looking machine that takes up only 12 inches of counter space.

Ninja sometimes has a reputation for doing too much, but we liked this semiautomatic as a beginner-friendly option that pulls some solid shots. It’s got a built-in grinder and milk frother, the latter of which can make cold foam and even has a setting for plant-based milk. In true Ninja fashion, it also has settings for drip coffee and cold brew, but neither impressed our tester, so I wouldn’t buy it for those features alone.

It has been revealed that former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested Terra Kaffe's newer Demi and mentioned it was perhaps the “dead-simplest fully automatic espresso machine I've yet encountered that still makes good coffee,” with just a dial and a button. Right now it's $200 off, or $300 off with a coffee subscription (Terra-Kaffe offers a house blend specifically made for use on its machines). Its bigger sibling, the TK-02, impressed our tester with its convenience, ease of use, front-facing water filter, and milk carafe. Though it didn't come out on top during a blind espresso taste test we did earlier this year, it's still a great-looking machine that's easy to use and is a whopping $400 off (or $500 with a coffee subscription) for Black Friday.

Atlas (3-month Gift subscription).

Atlas (6-month Gift subscription).

Maybe you or your recipient already has an espresso machine; in that case, they’ll need some quality beans. Our favorite coffee subscription, Atlas Coffee Club, has a new gift option on offer for Black Friday: a quarterly subscription of three bags of unique, globally sourced coffee every three months for $59. You can choose any roast you want, including espresso roast and even Nespresso pods. If you’d rather buy an ongoing subscription for yourself, your first bag is free with Atlas’ Black Friday sale.

Former barista and WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell likes this little scale that includes three magnetic add-ons: a platform, a metal dosing cup, and a catch cup that fits directly onto almost any portafilter.

If grounds are sticking to the plastic components of your coffee grinder, Cottell recommends adding this durable, stylish spray bottle to your espresso setup.

Cottell likes situating this mat underneath your espresso setup, as the lip contains spills and the textured portion is great for drying tools post-washing.

Some machines come with a tamper; others don't. If yours doesn’t, Cottell recommends you get this one. The spring-loaded base unloads 15 pounds of force to create a perfectly flat puck inside your portafilter. (A click lets you know when to stop pushing, so it’s great for beginners, too.).

Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed upcoming restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.
  • The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed upcoming restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, mentioned it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

Recent findings suggest that “We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based manufacturer had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#138959. Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2441 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise.
  • It has been revealed that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama.
  • But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

It has been revealed that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

In any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

According to recent reports, but I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

After college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech manufacturer willing to sponsor my green card. The problem was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

Industry observers note that the first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

In the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a fresh language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory company hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

Then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t latest. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

Industry observers note that I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Industry observers note that then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

Industry observers note that some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

For someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

While this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

Recent findings suggest that an operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

Industry observers note that but as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

Industry observers note that this means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.).

In a recent development, another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

Even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.).

One Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

Industry observers note that with this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning new languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

It has been revealed that I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

Industry observers note that this is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

"Deep tech" typically refers to developing cutting-edge technologies based on scientific research, such as AI, biotechnology and quantum computing.

A handful of massive fundraising rounds by firms including humanoid robot developer Neura Robotics,  AI drone maker Helsing and defense tech group Quantum Systems drove the investment boom.

Police in several locations across Germany reported large numbers of bomb threats targeting schools.

More than 400 schools in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg received threats, and more than 250 in Saxony-Anhalt received the emails, with several other regions also targeted on Monday morning.

Similar reports have also emerged to the north of Germany, in Denmark.

As in Germany, Danish police said they did not believe the threats were credible, "but they understandably create insecurity locally at the schools.".

Sources indicate that aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel room at the age of 55 with no foul play suspected. He's been the party's defining figure for almost four decades, having led the Free Voters to substantial success, especially in Bavaria.

The Free Voters are originally a grass roots party in Bavaria and sit on the conservative edge of the political spectrum. They've been in government in Bavaria as junior coaltion partners of the Christian Social Union (CSU), sister party to Chancellor Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

The strikes began on Friday and are due to continue until Tuesday. Wage negotiations are then set to continue on Wednesday with another round of collective bargaining for some 3.7 million workers across the sector.

The union is demanding a pay rise of 5% over one year while the employers association, Gesamtmetall, has offered a one-time payment and a pay increase of 1.3%.

A German investigative media report published on Monday claims that Russia would be able to launch a nuclear-armed satellite, called Sputnik-S, into orbit within the space of about 60 days if it wished.

The report from public broadcasters WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, cites a warning from German and other western intelligence agencies that it says was circulated at the start of November.

It said that a launch "could" take place by December, without quoting the document or clarifying whether it was talking only about a Russian capability, or a more firm intention.

The report said the satellite itself had been built several years ago and was being stored in the Moscow area.

German authorities did not respond to requests for comment on the record while the Russian Embassy in Berlin mentioned the claims were part of a "propaganda" campaign.

The report matches longstanding warnings, mainly but not exclusively from the US, that Russia could be preparing a nuclear strike in Earth orbit designed to take out a large number of satellites.

This could have a severe impact on intelligence, communications, logisticts, navigation and other key services.

Russia's war in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian military's reliance on the Starlink satellite internet service, has provided an additional reminder of the strategic significance of satellites in orbit.

What’s behind the growing demand are especially orders from South Africa, Egypt, Tunisia, Nigeria, Angola and Kenya — countries where inflation has been dropping and exchange rates are more stable.

In 2025, exports to Africa had risen by 8% while in 2024 it had gone down.

The Germangovernment has blamed oil and gas-producing nations for the COP climate conference ending without an agreement.

"The oil and gas industry is still dragging its feet," German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said after the UN climate talks had failed on Sunday. "Some oil-producing nations realize that the situation is becoming serious for them — that is why they are blocking it so vehemently," saidSchneider.

Almost two days into overtime, the COP31 climate talks in Turkey ended on Sunday as many countries, including the EU, rejected a final declaration.

Major sticking points at the summit included a commitment to accelerate global electrification and whether or not to explicitly mention aims to phase out fossil fuels. The suggested final declaration put forward by the COP presidency did not mention fossil fuels and according to critics would have undermined the shift away from fossil fuels.

"I understand that this poses a threat to the business model of those countries that sell us oil and gas. But electrification will make the world a more peaceful and stable place," Schneider said.

The inability to agree on a final declaration comes as climate change is increasingly linked to worsening heatwaves, floods and other natural catastrophes.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier begins a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya with a focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers.

He begins in Abidjan, where he is due to meet Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara. Steinmeier will also visit a vocational college and the International Academy for Counter-Terrorism before travelling on to Ghana.

In the capital Accra on Tuesday, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa.".

His final stop will be Kenya, where he will meet President William Ruto in Nairobi on Wednesday.

The German president is traveling with a German business delegation and wants to encourage closer economic ties and greater investment in Africa.

The trip is his 11th to sub-Saharan Africa and his final one as president as his term in office due to end next March.

And the country's president, Frank-Walter Steinmeier, is off for a trip to Africa which over the next few days that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

  • Akerson noted Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough.".

He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.

Akerson noted Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.

"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a substantial change.".

Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he noted the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable.".

According to recent reports, his comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.

Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.

According to recent reports, "Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he remarked.

The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.

Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.

Barra has remarked several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.

A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.

It has been revealed that GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.

That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates.".

When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he mentioned.

Akerson stated he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the tech giant, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.

Recent findings suggest that akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.

"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson remarked. "She's done a terrific job.".

Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.

Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.

Sources indicate that "This is crucial. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”.

Industry observers note that the price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

  • The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
  • The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
  • Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also stated that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

It has been revealed that problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

That caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a upcoming router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

Specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a new Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union noted that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

According to recent reports, similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

Sources indicate that to get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

(This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

It has been revealed that philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

As an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

According to recent reports, to kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

Recent findings suggest that and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

So you blueprint around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

According to recent reports, and even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

It has been revealed that it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a big network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

(Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

Industry observers note that so there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

It has been revealed that now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

Mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and says, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

So, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

Maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a new hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

Recent findings suggest that but this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

Sources indicate that it’s important to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

Mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has stated that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

According to recent reports, ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

But they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

It is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

It has been revealed that I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

It has been revealed that mann: An important caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

But what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not said it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

In a recent development, one of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

So in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

Do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that says a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

That’s the first big thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

Sources indicate that so it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the new router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

Then, and this is the important part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

That may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

Every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

Recent findings suggest that it is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

You’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

It has been revealed that in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

Ars Technica: The router installation matter that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

Industry observers note that mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

It’s not that they don’t want to modernize, and it’s not like the FAA doesn’t want to modernize. It’s just that it’s the old squeaky wheel thing, right? The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

In a recent development, actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live issue in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

According to recent reports, I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

Sources indicate that we could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

Recent findings suggest that mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. It decayed down to its essential mission, and preserved that essential mission at the expense of literally everything else.

It has been revealed that the apparent lack of risk analysis is a very clear example of the worst case scenario. The network-spanning maintenance being done in the middle of the day and allowed to cascade as a failure into the entire NAS, that was horrible. So a single set of technologies failed, but the NAS itself indicated its resilience in preserving that key mission all the way down to the minimum function, to the absolute zero, where the only piece left was just keep it safe. That’s what it’s supposed to do.

We don’t want to see it go that far down. We’d much rather have them just divert flights a couple minutes here and there. But if we need to get it all the way down to the only thing we have is safe aircraft, I’m good with that.

Sources indicate that ars Technica: Duffy is saying the FAA needs $50 billion to make sure this doesn’t happen again. And if I understood correctly, you were saying it is good to have support for enough funding for the FAA to do what it needs to do, even if Duffy tying it specifically to “this happened because we didn’t have enough money” is not necessarily the correct assessment.

Mann: Yeah. This happened because there wasn’t the right oversight. I’d be pretty confident to say that. If we just take $50 billion and throw it at the same people doing the same thing the same way, we don’t get a better system. We just get a whole bunch more of this.

Recent findings suggest that because hiring more contractors and getting more routers replaced faster in the middle of the day with no risk assessment and incorrect configurations or however it came about… take some of that money and put it into oversight, put it into testing, and put it into whatever you need to do to make sure that however many more of these we’re going to do are done properly, and in this case, at 2 o’clock in the morning with a team of qualified people with the proper testing, people ready to pull a plug on it, all that kind of stuff. That’s money well spent.

It has been revealed that ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router issue that led to the ground stop. The FAA has stated the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

Sources indicate that mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

Recent findings suggest that now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

Sources indicate that if you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

It has been revealed that but you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

But the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

To the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

It has been revealed that SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and claims, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

#138947. A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

A Power Provider for Meta Urged Regulators to Exempt Data Center Plants From Acid Rain Rules

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1509 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.
  • The oil and gas infrastructure manufacturer’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.
  • In a recent development, “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Williams, a provider of gas power to several Meta data centers, met with Environmental Protection Agency leaders in the period leading up to the agency’s recommendation to waive acid rain regulations for data-center power plants, documents obtained by WIRED show.

The oil and gas infrastructure manufacturer’s private discussions with the agency come as the Trump administration loosens a number of environmental requirements for data centers and the natural gas plants being built to power them.

In a recent development, “The administration is trying to relax, if not suspend for all intents and purposes, a range of regulatory requirements for these data centers,” says Joseph Goffman, the former assistant administrator at the EPA’s Office of Air and Radiation. “What this administration is trying to do, either explicitly or de facto, is take layers [of regulatory protections] away.”.

In response to a list of questions from WIRED, Williams spokesperson Alex Schott said in an emailed statement that the company “is committed to developing energy solutions to enhance America’s position in the global competition for AI, while prioritizing environmental protection—including addressing legislation and regulations to modernize construction and implementation timelines.” Meta declined to comment.

Recent findings suggest that in July, the EPA announced upcoming federal guidance for states around participation in the Acid Rain Program, following inquiries from “companies and States.” The decades-old program was designed to reduce harmful emissions of chemicals that cause acid rain. Power plants that fall under the program need to submit a permit application two years before a facility comes online, and then regularly monitor emissions to ensure compliance.

According to recent reports, that month, the EPA stated that it recommends that “islanded” power plants—which are increasingly being adopted by data centers across the country—be exempt from the program. Because the program was designed for facilities that sell electricity to the grid, the EPA said, power plants that exclusively power data centers wouldn’t need to comply.

Documents obtained by WIRED from the EPA show that Williams was one of three private companies that asked regulators for guidance on the program.

In a February letter sent to the Utah Department of Environmental Quality and obtained by WIRED, Williams director of permitting Steve Hall wrote that the “current regulatory uncertainty” around power plants being built solely to power data centers has created “obstacles … for data center development in the United States.” The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams sent the agency this letter.

Hall wrote that the organization believed its power plants “are not subject to the Acid Rain Permit program requirements, as this program was never intended to apply to sources that do not sell power to the public grid.” Getting federal guidance, he wrote, would “accelerate deployment of critical infrastructure” and “support national goals for digital infrastructure and energy reliability in the global AI race.”.

It has been revealed that the EPA said in its July announcement that the fresh guidance was in keeping with orders from the White House to encourage data center developers to build their own power, in order to avoid increasing utility rates for consumers. However, data center developers are also increasingly turning to private power because it’s often quicker to build their own infrastructure than wait for a grid connection. These private power plants often create more emissions than many of their on-grid counterparts.

Industry observers note that williams, one of the top oil and gas infrastructure companies in the country, has emerged in recent years as a power provider for data centers. As of November, Williams had at least six data-center power plant projects in states across the country. Meta is the client for at least four of those projects: four in Ohio, and one in Utah.

Calendar invites provided by EPA show that Hall and other executives were invited to at least two meetings with EPA officials, including at least one with Aaron Szabo, then the chief of the agency’s Air office, earlier this year. In an external meeting request form filed with the agency in April, Williams indicated that its request to discuss projects in Ohio and Utah—sites where it is building power plants for Meta—was “urgent.”.

The EPA confirmed to WIRED that Williams “requested regulatory guidance for both projects” in Ohio and Utah, and that the meetings “broadly discussed air regulations.”.

“EPA program offices regularly meet with stakeholders in their areas of jurisdiction,” the agency added.

Industry observers note that williams’ materials submitted to regulators did not specifically reference its relationship with Meta. But in its official letter on the rule recommendations, the EPA used an example provided by an unnamed manufacturer that is building a planned 500-megawatt power plant of simple-cycle natural gas engines “to exclusively power an adjacent, third-party-owned data center.” Williams’ project in Utah and two of its projects in Ohio to power Meta data centers are around 500 megawatts each.

Williams first publicly proposed the exemption to the Acid Rain Program in September 2025 in testimony to the House of Representatives from Mark Gebbia, then the organization’s vice president of environmental, permitting, and regulatory affairs. In the testimony, Gebbia made several suggestions as to how EPA should change or clarify the implementation of the Clean Air Act, including exempting behind-the-meter data centers from Acid Rain Program requirements. He noted that the long timelines for the permits are “not feasible given the urgent need to install and operate gas-fired generation for AI data centers.”.

It has been revealed that the Acid Rain Program has long been considered a regulatory success that’s ensured coal plants reduce emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, pollutants that help create acid rain. The law created a cap-and-trade program for power plants, allowing them to buy and sell credits for emissions to keep national levels of the pollutants low.

According to recent reports, natural gas plants emit lower levels of these pollutants than traditional coal-fired power plants. The permit application for Williams’ facility to power Meta’s data center in Utah, for example, shows that it could emit a maximum of around 100 tons of nitrogen oxide and 11 tons of sulfur dioxide each year. A 500-megawatt coal plant, meanwhile, can emit thousands of tons per year of each of those pollutants.

Other local and national restrictions may limit how much of these pollutants come from natural gas plants. But Acid Rain Program regulations also created crucial reporting requirements that are now in jeopardy for data-center power plants. In the early 1990s, Congress passed an amendment to the Clean Air Act mandating that power facilities monitor and report various emissions in order to establish the program. The reporting requirement covers sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, as well as carbon dioxide, the main driver of climate change.

The Obama administration later set up a program that would separate CO2 reporting requirements, though the Trump administration has made moves to repeal that program.

Now, exempting data-center power plants from complying with the acid rain regulations may jeopardize how much information regulators eventually get about data center emissions—including CO2 emissions, Goffman says.

“If the Trump administration was not deranged, and the greenhouse gas reporting program was operating, I think the EPA would be either interpreting that program’s existing requirements to cover these gas plants, or they would be promulgating upcoming regulations to ensure these new gas plants were reporting their greenhouse gas emissions,” he says.

It has been revealed that both Goffman and Carrie Jenks, who directs the Environmental and Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, agree that the EPA’s guidance on the Acid Rain Program for data centers seems to stick to the letter of the law. The program, they say, was explicitly intended to apply only to power plants that sold power to the grid. (Some environmental groups disagree with Goffman and Jenks: Earthjustice and the NRDC sent a letter to the EPA in September challenging the agency’s interpretation of the law in its July recommendation.).

When the program was created in 1990, though, wealthy tech companies weren’t rushing to build hundreds of megawatts of private fossil-fuel power that may not ever be connected to the grid. “No one expected it to be economical to develop a bunch of power plants that wouldn’t sell the product they were creating. No one envisioned this,” Jenks indicates. The program “was never designed to address behind-the-meter generation,” she says.

According to recent reports, some estimates show that there’s more than 110 gigawatts of planned behind-the-meter gas projects in the US, with some facilities—like Amazon’s 7-gigawatt facility in Texas, and SoftBank’s 9.2-gigawatt project in Ohio—on track to be some of the largest natural gas plants in the world. Even if those facilities don’t technically qualify for the Acid Rain Program because they’re not on the grid, lawmakers could move to change requirements to make sure that these massive facilities are covered by the program.

According to recent reports, “Congress should have the ability and the authority to say, we have this situation, it wasn’t anticipated, here is the law,” Jenks says. “If the world were working, that’s what should happen.”.
