📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector.

According to recent reports, lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her latest office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers.

According to recent reports, leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic â which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries â are based here. Anthropic, the firm behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

But what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting substantial fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Industry observers note that concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (Â£49bn).

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal.

Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring.

Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now?

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco â no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles â be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker, employed by one of the largest companies in the city, is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come downâ¦ and I'm sure it will affect me," states the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?".

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, indicates that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

According to recent reports, yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he claims that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great.".

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

In a recent development, for all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new manufacturer formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Industry observers note that instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

It has been revealed that nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he states.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI.

But AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism â which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness â are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," claims Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

Industry observers note that "The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he claims. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy.".

According to recent reports, as to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking organization owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes â "always a reality in San Francisco" â she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she notes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a Sunday morning in April, minutes from the US Capitol and down a stretch of Washington, DC’s Pennsylvania Avenue, a wall of black SUVs lined up alongside yellow police tape. Men in military gear held long guns and guarded the entrance to a mirrored window and door.

This is Christ Church DC, a place of worship that appeared on Capitol Hill a year ago.

That Sunday, high-ranking government officials, including Homeland Security's intelligence chief, America’s top international health diplomat, and the government’s international finance chief, had gathered to hear a sermon. “It gives a whole upcoming meaning to worshipping in the presence of your enemies,” quipped the pastor, referencing the church’s location. “We’ve asked the government to fix us, and we’re more enslaved than ever.”.

Christ Church DC arrived after Pete Hegseth, who regularly attends worship with his family, was confirmed as US secretary of defense.

The church is part of Pastor Doug Wilson’s network, known as the CREC—the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches—which is headquartered in Moscow, Idaho. Wilson’s long-held goal is to turn America into a theocracy, where all its institutions are molded in accordance with biblical law, executions are made public, non-Christians are barred from holding office, and women submit to their husbands instead of voting.

WIRED has identified around a dozen government officials who have attended services at Christ Church DC at least once since it opened a year ago. Other officials who have attended include a top-ranking Pentagon adviser, a former senior Marine Corps pilot who now oversees personnel affairs in the Navy, and a federal immigration judge with a history of attracting complaints of volatile outbursts toward colleagues.

Sources indicate that wilson calls DC “Babylon on the Potomac,” a biblical moniker he uses to evoke a corrupt place populated by ungodly people. The church has occupied three different locations since it was established, and Wilson has been raising funds to buy a permanent home for it. “We are here for the long haul,” he wrote in a blog post earlier this year. “We believe that it is our responsibility to begin pursuing opportunities to purchase a building near Capitol Hill.” He has also advised on his podcast to not “go to DC and go native” and “[climb] the greasy pole of ambition.” Rather, he stated DC “needs an infusion of God-fearing humans.”.

Industry observers note that wilson, who initially agreed to an interview with WIRED and then abruptly canceled with little explanation, hasn’t shied away in past media engagements from touting his newfound clout in government circles. “This is the first time we’ve had connections with as many people in national government as we do now,” Wilson told the Associated Press in 2025, shortly after he came to DC to speak at the opening of his new church.

Wilson’s rising profile and expansion to DC wouldn’t have been possible without Hegseth, says Peter Bell, a researcher, theologian, and host of the podcast Sons of Patriarchy, which has been investigating Wilson for years. “Hegseth gave them an in.”.

“The secretary is a proud member of a church affiliated with the Congregation of Reformed Evangelical Churches, which was founded by Pastor Doug Wilson,” chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell told WIRED in response to a request for comment. “The secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson’s writings and teachings.”.

It has been revealed that parnell subsequently issued a second statement. “Staff at the Department of War have the liberty to practice their faith and attend any church they choose,” he remarked, using the administration’s name for the Defense Department. “It is shameful that WIRED is attempting to smear respected personnel for exercising their religious freedoms.”.

In 2022, well before he was nominated to President Donald Trump’s cabinet, Hegseth moved his family to the Nashville, Tennessee, area to attend a CREC church and enroll his children in an affiliated classical Christian school. After he was narrowly confirmed as secretary of defense last year, Hegseth introduced a regular monthly Pentagon prayer service and brought out his pastor from Tennessee, Brooks Potteiger, to lead the inaugural session. In July, Potteiger officially became the pastor of Christ Church DC.

“I believe this is significant,” Potteiger said on a podcast with Wilson and other church elders before his move to DC. “It energizes me … to see these young families, and especially the young Christian men, who are hungry for a soaring biblical view of the lordship of Christ over all things.” (Christ Church DC did not respond to WIRED’s request for an interview with Potteiger.).

Sources indicate that as secretary, Hegseth has invoked scripture when talking about the war in Iran, established an office of religious affairs at the Pentagon, and used his position to claim that America is a fundamentally Christian nation. "Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual," Hegseth said in a speech in late September. "Live your calling. Stand firm. Preach truth. Minister to the flock." He has invited Wilson to speak at Pentagon prayer sessions twice this year. In Wilson’s most recent address to the military, just last week, he told his audience why they are right to want America to become a theocracy and why they are right to want to impose a Christian conservative social order.

Wilson, who describes himself as “paleo-Confederate,” has been a fringe figure for decades and operates within a grab bag of historical Protestant traditions. He’s been seeding his influence through his network of around 160 churches and hundreds of CREC-accredited schools and colleges across the US and internationally, laying the groundwork to take his blueprint for a Christian nationalist society well beyond Idaho. Wilson has made it explicitly clear that he is building toward a fresh political and social order in America—one that places the church at its center and is ruled by Christian men.

Through various affiliated media outlets, Wilson has said “women need to be pastored, and they need to be pastored by men,” and as recently as 2024 he advocated for the repeal of the 19th Amendment, which gave women the right to vote. This belief system goes back decades: In 1996 he coauthored a booklet describing slavery as a “relationship based upon mutual affection and confidence.” He has said that he doesn’t believe that “a Muslim should be able to hold political office” and called immigration a “deliberately fomented war on the American heritage and unremitting hostility to the culture.”.

Wilson’s reach into the US government now extends beyond Hegseth. Christ Church DC’s latest worshipers include Justin Overbaugh, deputy undersecretary of war for intelligence and security at the Defense department; Nate Halverson, chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs; C. Scott “Sonny” Duncan, senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy; Stuart Scheller, senior adviser to the US undersecretary of war for personnel and readiness; and Ryan Higgins, senior adviser for religious complications at the Pentagon and one of Hegseth’s key aides.

Overbaugh, a former US Army officer who was working in risk management in Florida until Hegseth nominated him, now deals with highly sensitive military intelligence and counterintelligence. Overbaugh is an attendee of Christ Church DC and is slated to give a seminar in Tampa, Florida, in January titled “Serving Christ in the Pentagon.”.

Sources indicate that halverson graduated from New Saint Andrews College, a university in Moscow, Idaho, that Wilson cofounded, in 2006. In October, despite having no military background, Halverson was appointed chief of staff to the assistant secretary of the Navy for manpower and reserve affairs, another senior Pentagon leadership role that is involved with recruiting all Navy and Marine Corps personnel and oversees policies that impact all military and civilian personnel and their families within the Navy. Prior to joining the Pentagon, Halverson spent 15 years working in sales for Verint, a workforce management software company.

Duncan, who describes himself as “executive servant leader” on his LinkedIn, was recently promoted to senior counselor to the secretary of the Navy, an influential position that allows him to help shape decisions that impact the entirety of US Navy operations. Duncan is a former Marine pilot who retired in 2023 to fly commercial American Airlines planes and work part-time at Chick-fil-A. His decision to retire with the rank of lieutenant colonel was borne out of his objection to the military’s Covid-19 vaccine requirements, which in turn garnered him positive attention in right-wing media circles.

Last year, Hegseth made Duncan a key point of contact for an initiative titled “Reinstating Service Members Negatively Impacted by the Coronavirus Disease 2019 Vaccination Mandate.”.

Scheller, a former Marine who reached the rank of lieutenant colonel, was court-martialed in 2021 after pleading guilty to showing contempt and disrespect for senior military officials over the chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan. Higgins, who has also attended the church, was revealed in a recent CNN investigation to have shared scores of racist and homophobic social media posts targeting immigrants and Muslims. Higgins has also played a key role in shaping Hegseth’s Christian nationalist messaging at the Pentagon, CNN reported.

According to recent reports, according to data from 2019, 70 percent of active-duty service members identified as Christian. Mikey Weinstein, a former Air Force officer, attorney, and founder of the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, estimates that around half of those adhere to Christian nationalist ideology. For many of those, he thinks that it’s a case of emulating the ideology that they are seeing from their leaders. Weinstein indicates that the vast majority of the service members that his organization represents are Christians who feel alarmed by and powerless to push back against Christian nationalism that’s taken hold at all ranks, including at the very top.

Government officials outside of the Pentagon are also involved with Christ Church DC.

Sources indicate that trump administration couple Bethany and Matthew Kozma have attended the church with their children. Bethany Kozma, the director of global affairs at the Department of Health and Human Services—America's top international health diplomat—is known for her positions against abortion and transgender rights. Matthew Kozma is the Department of Homeland Security's undersecretary for intelligence and analysis and oversees all concerns related to “counterterrorism, counterproliferation of weapons of mass destruction, and critical infrastructure protection.” Both Bethany and Matthew were contributors to Project 2025.

The church has also attracted some personnel from the Justice Department, including David Vandenberg, who was hired to the DOJ’s civil rights division last year and was seated last month as an immigration judge. He worked in Upcoming Mexico and Texas as an assistant US attorney from 2021 to 2024. In Texas, Vandenberg’s colleagues complained of alleged volatile behavior.

Recent findings suggest that brantley Mayers, a former fellow at the Claremont Institute, a right-wing think tank, works as counsel to the assistant attorney general for the DOJ’s civil division. Mayers was often a spokesperson for the DOJ, defending the Trump administration’s ICE occupation of Minneapolis earlier this year. He was also referred for discipline in June after a federal judge ruled that the DOJ had engaged in “unsettling” practices in its efforts to get a Rhode Island hospital to comply with a subpoena over transgender care. “That is dirty pool, in my opinion, and the Department of Justice have willfully done that in this case,” the judge remarked at a May 2026 hearing. Mayers represented the DOJ at a hearing for this case.

It has been revealed that another church attendee is Stephen Duggan, chief financial officer at the US International Development Finance Corporation, which invests in private-sector development projects overseas. (Earlier this year, the head of the DFC was questioned by Congressional Democrats about the agency’s investments and their “potential entanglements” with the Trump family.) In the past, Duggan worked as the chief financial officer for Bentkey Ventures, a subscription-based streaming service that offers “anti-woke” children’s content and is owned by the media organization The Daily Wire.

According to recent reports, andrew Braun, defense policy adviser for Mike Rounds, a GOP senator from South Dakota and former government relations manager at the conservative think tank The Heritage Foundation, has also attended church services. Paul Lindstrom, who was briefly an offensive lineman for the University of Idaho Vandals football team and worked as an executive assistant in the Office of the President until recently, has attended, as has Samuel Brown, undersecretary for memorial affairs at the Department of Veterans Affairs.

(WIRED reached out to all the government officials mentioned in this story for comment. None of them replied with the exception of a spokesperson for Bethany Kozma, who initially denied that she’d ever attended the church. When told that WIRED was entirely confident that Kozma had attended at least once, the spokesperson said she would call back and never did.).

At the church, these officials rub shoulders with members of conservative think tanks, delegates from the CREC network, judicial clerks, venture capitalists, lobbyists, and more.

Sources indicate that having like-minded Christians in office is a core part of Wilson’s long-term strategy. “Wilson is explicit concerning his desire to see Christians in office—and only Christians in office—and a church at the foot of the Capitol is the clearest route toward that end,” says Bell.

It has been revealed that A core part of Project 2025, the blueprint for Trump’s second term in office, was a strategy to infuse Christian nationalist ideology into all levels of US government. Shortly after taking office, Trump signed an executive order that established a task force to investigate “anti-Christian bias” in government departments, and Christian nationalists were placed in key roles. Across the government, and beyond the Pentagon, this attitude has been replicated: The former secretary of labor began a monthly prayer service months after the creation of a White House Faith Office.

“Doug, in his own words, has always specified a Christian culture comes from the ground up rather than being imposed, and that is crucial here,” said Bell. “Put Christians in office, legislate Christian morality, let that simmer among the populace, and Christian culture eventually emerges.”.

A human liver has been kept alive outside the body for a record seven weeks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1038 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.
  • The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.
  • In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in Australia claim they’ve kept a human liver alive, on life support, outside the body for seven weeks, opening up speculative new possibilities in biomedical engineering.

The feat, whose details are pending publication, was carried out in Sydney after a team led by surgeon and inventor Carlo Pulitano connected a donated liver to a system of automated pumps and sensors that fed the organ nutrients, supplied it with blood, and whisked away waste.

In an interview, Pulitano, a transplant surgeon at the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and a professor at the University of Sydney, likened the life support system to “an artificial body.” Its official name is the Extended Organ Perfusion System.

“Our group is the only one in the world to have maintained a human liver under fully normothermic, physiological conditions for seven weeks,” he indicates.

Normothermic means body temperature, or about 37 °C. The previous record for keeping an internal organ alive outside the body was set in Switzerland several years ago. That organ—also a liver—lasted around two weeks.

In a recent development, most organs destined for transplant survive only a few hours in special ice buckets and need to be raced to their destination. Over the last decade, however, surgeons have been switching to perfusion systems, which pump warm or cold fluids into an organ. This can double the time it can be held before it must be transplanted.

According to recent reports, pulitano says the key to breaking the record was to automate the systems used to keep the organ thriving. During a meeting in Switzerland earlier this year, the Sydney team described perfusing 55 human livers, one after the other. Some were connected to a system that needed to be adjusted manually, but for those placed on the automated system—which produced the seven-week survivor—the average survival time tripled, to about four weeks.

Perfusion has already enabled doctors to restart hearts from dead people and keep them beating outside the body. Paulo Martins, a transplant doctor at the University of Oklahoma, notes about half the kidneys he transplants are now perfused, even though the process can add $100,000 to the cost of a transplant.

While the research awaits formal publication, the eventual goal is what Pulitano and colleagues call “time-unlimited liver preservation.”.

Scientists have already discovered possible medical benefits to keeping organs on life support longer than usual. One, they say, is that perfused organs apparently start to repair themselves and become stronger after a day or so. That’s what led a Swiss team, in 2022, to transplant a damaged liver that had been kept on perfusion for three days—the longest time any internal organ had remained outside the body before a successful transplant, says Waldemar Hoffmann, the CEO and cofounder of Apersys, a startup formed to commercialize the technology.

Pulitano states his own startup, Aeternum Life Technologies, will be helping with a planned trial in Sydney to transplant low-quality livers kept on perfusion for four days.

In a recent development, what’s less clear, says Hoffmann, is whether any transplant surgeon would ever want, or need, to use an organ kept alive for nearly two months. He says people in the field believe Pulitano’s record is real, but they don’t know how healthy the organ was at the end or even what so much extra time is likely to achieve. “The key question is what the purpose for a seven-week perfusion would be,” he says.

According to recent reports, yet that’s where things could start to get interesting, says Martins, the Oklahoma surgeon. Long-term life support could enable far-out concepts like artificial wombs, new types of organ manufacturing, and the chance to experiment directly on human organs outside the body for extended periods.

For his part, Pulitano says long-term machine perfusion could help grow latest organs. In living donations, surgeons commonly take half of a person’s liver to give someone else. After about two months, both parts will have grown back almost to their full volume. Pulitano says he’s tried dividing a liver and then attaching the sections to the machine. If that works, he says, it could be a way to multiply one donor liver into several full-size organs.

“It’s notable to have people thinking outside the box and pushing the limits and creating possibilities for things that, right now, sometimes we don’t even have a need for but are going to be needed in the future,” states Martins. “That’s how science moves.”.

Sources indicate that he’s not the only one who thinks so. For instance, a US tech giant, Bexorg, has been reanimating human brains using perfusion pumps. The idea is to study what effects experimental drugs have on them. That company perfuses brains for about a day but has said it wants to extend the time to two weeks.

Similar experiments can be done on livers, says Pulitano, who has already tried adding gene therapies to the organs. “It gives us a living human organ model for translational research that no animal system can match, because the biology, the immunology, and the drug responses are human from the outset,” he says.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in Silicon Valley, patents filed by Altos Labs, a billionaire-backed longevity startup, describe attempts to introduce reprogramming genes into animal livers maintained outside the body. Eventually, Altos scientists have speculated, they might temporarily disconnect a failing organ while it’s still in a person’s body, connecting it to a perfusion machine in order to douse it with ultra-powerful genetic treatments without risking the rest of the body.

In a recent development, doctors probing the limits of organ life support have now formed two fresh scientific societies to explore the concept. One, founded by Martins and called the International Society for Organ Preservation and Perfusion Therapy, will hold its inaugural meeting this year in Italy. The other, based in China, was released in August to advance what doctors at the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University have termed “organ medicine”: research at the level of whole organs kept alive by “bionic maintenance.”.

According to recent reports, “What is exploding is the idea of this technology that clearly goes beyond simply organ preservation,” indicates Pulitano. “Basically, that’s a concept that’s entirely new.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report shows.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, upcoming report shows. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an important purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

However, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

There is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

In a recent development, “The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Industry observers note that jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, noted she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the firm launched and published “The Never List,” which at the moment cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

In a recent development, “Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

In a recent development, “We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

According to recent reports, most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic remarked. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Recent findings suggest that single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

“Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

Sources indicate that however, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt noted. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply problems posed a challenge, forcing it to at the moment aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

According to recent reports, “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

Beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

Sources indicate that “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” stated Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Recent findings suggest that sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is presently facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a firm on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is currently completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, notes her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high indicates the scale of India's climate challenge.

Industry observers note that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann remarked. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

Industry observers note that and when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, claims the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

Sources indicate that “Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability problems) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she said. “Market leadership is key.”.

In the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

Latest Update: Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.
  • Industry observers note that in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures.
  • Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius.".

Industry observers note that in the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention.".

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch.".

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

It has been revealed that at the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also demonstrates where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

Industry observers note that that means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us.".

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," states van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013. How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," notes van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery.".

In a recent development, the samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again.".

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist states that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'".

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project.".

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

The rise and fall and rise again of Jensen Huang

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.
  • Sources indicate that then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market.
  • Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's being called a comeback for the ages.

For a long time it seemed that Jensen Huang, the leather jacket-clad founder of Nvidia, dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech", could do no wrong.

Sources indicate that then came allegations of two affairs - one with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy - that rocked the world of tech and the global stock market. Huang resigned.

Now, just 11 days later, he's been reinstated by the board, who says it believes he is the right person to lead the organization.

So what do we know about the man who is once again at the head of Nvidia, a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China?

Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

Sources indicate that but his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the fresh technology.

The firm is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.

Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession saw him amass an estimated fortune of close to $200bn earlier this year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, though that has since dropped to around $105bn.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.

They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

Industry observers note that the firm became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a fresh direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation.

Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?

Huang has hailed AI as a "latest industrial revolution" that is on a par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

According to recent reports, "Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".

But while Huang is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he mentioned.

Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very notable to him".

Sources indicate that first reports emerged on 29 October in the Latest York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.

Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by an announcement that Huang was stepping down.

He'd barely been gone, however, before a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign was rolled out, reportedly by current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters.

The man himself noted he would be "honoured" to return, should the board ask him.

Although initially showing no interest in reinstating him, the board has now done just that, saying his return was "in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Somehow, Jensen Huang returned.

A mere 12 days after the controversial, embattled Nvidia CEO was ousted from his position, the substantial tech firm announced that he would be reinstated. Coincidentally or not, this decision followed Donald Trump's public endorsement of Huang's return. Regardless of how or why it happened, the big question now is how NVDA will respond on the stock market.

Needless to say, if you're an Nvidia shareholder, you're probably feeling pretty all right on Monday morning. At the time of publication, NVDA is up a staggering 35 percent from the start of trading. This came after a tech sell-off last week, which might explain the huge percentage jump. The current price of $170 per share isn't much higher than the $162 level it was at early last week before the sell-off, but it's obviously significantly higher than the $125 price it ended the week at.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

In a recent development, the timeline of Huang's resignation is messy and convoluted. It started with the revelation that he was having an extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, though there is reason to believe she may not have been an intelligence asset. Regardless, a second affair with a subordinate Nvidia executive came to light, which led to his resignation almost two weeks ago.

#138900. Breaking: NASA’s newly introduced Moon strategy is taking shape, but some big questions remain

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: NASA’s newly introduced Moon strategy is taking shape, but some big questions remain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2322 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-key, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
  • For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
  • Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-key, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

According to recent reports, the Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Industry observers note that other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

In a recent development, ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

According to recent reports, for Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a Upcoming Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

It has been revealed that NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

According to recent reports, so, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

It has been revealed that “The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech noted. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

Industry observers note that “With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech stated. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”.

Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech noted. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”.

The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

It has been revealed that “With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech remarked. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”.

In a recent development, while there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

NASA levied latest test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company plans to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

It has been revealed that “One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech mentioned. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

In a recent development, this year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight proposal for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech stated. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”.

The upcoming concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

According to recent reports, “One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech said. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”.

In a recent development, the six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

Recent findings suggest that now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

In a recent development, what’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

It has been revealed that “We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”.

Recent findings suggest that for missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated plans do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four launches of the tech giant’s Newly introduced Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

Sources indicate that A new stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

Starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech stated, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

Starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each organization’s uncrewed landing demos.

For now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

“Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech said. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”.

It has been revealed that that could change. Today’s proposal gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

According to recent reports, “When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” mentioned Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”.

For Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one launched from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

“The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a big learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”.

It has been revealed that the propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

Industry observers note that that is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

According to recent reports, the low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling launches. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

According to recent reports, for context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

SpaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk stated Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent enhancement to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech said.

#138899. Latest Update: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware
