8 Windows apps you should probably remove from your PC

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1374 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not every app on your PC deserves a permanent place.
  • According to recent reports, bloatware and adware aren't upcoming, but they feel far more prevalent these days.
  • The ubiquity of these annoyances, including junk built into Windows itself, means that debloating a fresh Windows PC has become a common practice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not every app on your PC deserves a permanent place.

According to recent reports, bloatware and adware aren't upcoming, but they feel far more prevalent these days. Not only do they take up SSD space (which is more precious than ever because of soaring storage prices), but they can also consume RAM and annoy you with alerts you don't care about.

The ubiquity of these annoyances, including junk built into Windows itself, means that debloating a fresh Windows PC has become a common practice. Some apps (both preinstalled and common third-party tools), aren't actively detrimental. But, depending on how you use your PC, it may be worth upgrading them with superior — and often inexpensive or free — options. Here are several such Windows apps you should replace or remove outright.

Media Player, not to be confused with the classic Windows Media Player from prior Windows versions, is the out-of-the-box way to listen to music or watch videos on your PC. And while it does a suitable job of playing both audio and video files from a broad range of formats, it can't compete with the features you get from alternative apps like VLC.

VLC can play tons of video formats (even rare ones) without the need for additional codecs or extensions. It can also handle media file conversions quickly and easily. If you love subtitles but have a video file that lacks them, VLC can take dragged-and-dropped .srt or .vtt files from the web. The totally-free app can do so much more once you dig into it.

It's never been easier to get into content creation, which can blossom into a potentially profitable side hustle. Even if not, it's fun sharing your creativity with close friends and anyone the algorithm pushes you towards. Microsoft Clipchamp is included in Windows 11 and offers a user-friendly way to crop, cut and edit videos in up to 1080p. Unfortunately, it keeps a lot of its flashier features, like Copilot integration and 4K exporting, along with access to premium stock assets, filters and effects, behind the Microsoft 365 paywall.

It has been revealed that as someone who edits video almost every day, it's difficult for me to recommend anything else but CapCut to amateur creators. It's approachable for beginners while also providing plenty of features that professionals will love. And as someone leery about shoehorned AI features, I find those in CapCut actually useful (some of them, anyway).

There's a subscription here too if you want to take full advantage, starting at $19.99 per month. But it's one of the few apps on this payment model that provides substantial value.

While it might sound shallow to say, uTorrent is one of the most hideous-looking modern apps. Like many programs that offer free versions, it's full of ads and foists extra junk apps on you during installation. In 2015, uTorrent received backlash after it secretly installed Epic Scale, a Litecoin miner, with every new installation. We're more than a decade removed from this, but it's the kind of cynical action that people never really forget.

There are countless replacements, with two highlights depending on what you're after. For a uTorrent-like experience without the bloat or ads, there's qBittorrent. It's got a slightly larger footprint than uTorrent, has built-in search engines, and is widely accepted on private trackers. If you prefer a slimmed-down, barebones approach, Transmission is hard to beat.

Setting up a latest PC is exciting, but also comes with some frustrations. You'll probably be dismayed to see, after dropping big bucks on a new piece of tech, that you still have to contend with pre-installed software like Norton or McAfee. It's annoying to get bombarded with alerts that your trial (which you never wanted) is ending, especially since Windows Defender is more than enough for most people.

Recent findings suggest that considering how good Defender is, McAfee, Norton, and other antivirus apps don't simply provide protection from viruses. Their paid versions add other security services such as a VPN, scam detection and support for restoring your identity if it's stolen. But if you're just looking for bog-standard protection from viruses, Defender should be vigilant enough to keep your PC safe.

Does anyone actually use these? Despite their default presence in the world's most popular desktop OS, I've never once heard of anyone actually implementing the built-in news and weather apps in their regular workflow. It's almost impressive that Microsoft still supports these, which probably see less regular use than Minesweeper.

The Weather app isn't terrible, but there's nothing particularly exciting about it and it also has annoying ads to work around. Plenty of weather sites give you more data in a cleaner experience. The News app is considerably worse, cramming tons of low-quality and clickbait stories amongst more ads. You'll have far better results curating a feed with RSS, following your favorite news publications on social media or getting alerts from their dedicated apps.

Industry observers note that while Xbox still has dedicated consoles, Microsoft's dedicated gaming brand has taken on a more nebulous definition. It's a console, but also an app and a store, with games you can stream to many other devices. If you're a gamer, the Xbox app for Windows has plenty of features and tools like Xbox mode that come close to providing a console-like experience with the power of your PC. It's constantly updated, supports cloud gaming, lets you easily connect with friends and aggregates all your games from various storefronts in one convenient place.

Industry observers note that but if you're not a gamer, it does little more than take up resources. Even if you are a gamer, those who stick to Steam for their games can get by without the Xbox app. That's also the case for anyone who's hopped off the Game Pass bandwagon recently.

In a recent development, if you want a simple example of how cynical adware has gotten in recent years, just remind yourself that in the not-too-distant past, Minesweeper and Solitaire came standard with every copy of Windows and weren't bogged down with ads like they are today. You can pay for the premium edition of Microsoft Solitaire Collection for $1.49 per month, which won't break the bank, but still feels unnecessarily rent-seeking.

But with games as simple as these, there are, luckily, many free alternatives easily accessible from your web browser. Solitaire for Free and Minesweeper for Free are exactly what they're poised as: classic versions of these games with no nonsense. Minesweeper doesn't offer much customization outside of difficulty, but Solitaire has more than 30 variations, plus light customization of its cards and background.

Industry observers note that if you want an alternative that you can play offline, Free Solitaire on Steam is tough to beat. There are tons of different game modes and variants, lots of card customization (including personalized art if you want) and zero ads.

It has been revealed that one of the irrefutable facts of life is that "nothing beats free." Sure, there are outliers, but if I had to cite my source for this ancient adage, it would be Google Docs and the rest of Google Workspace. Google's productivity suite features everything most people need for personal documents, spreadsheets and presentations. And web links make them easy to share with whoever needs them.

It's not a one-to-one match for Microsoft Office, which is why many professionals still need the full Microsoft suite. Microsoft Office extensions like .docx and .xlsx are the corporate standard, and while Google Docs can export to these, doing so can result in some wonky formatting.

Unfortunately, accessing Microsoft Office applications requires paying at least $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for Microsoft 365. If you prefer the feel of a dedicated app, or are leery of letting Google take over another part of your life, there are plenty of great Microsoft Office alternatives. One is OnlyOffice, which provides a comparable Office experience while also being free (with paid options for businesses and developers).

No matter which option you choose, you can uninstall the free Microsoft Office trials that come with Windows and only serve to push you into signing up for a subscription when you open an Office file.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.
  • It has been revealed that it would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media reports, citing two people briefed on the problem.

The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks.

It has been revealed that it would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US. The agency did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Industry observers note that when asked about the breach in a Fox News interview on Saturday, President Donald Trump said he had "just heard" about the hack. "I will say that it's not good. I don't like that," he said.

"But maybe we'll learn things that we would've never learned otherwise," Trump added.

According to recent reports, this apparent breach of FBI database comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have stated they were not caused by cyber-attacks, but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with Trump saying he was not good enough.

Dan Lorhmann, a former analyst for the National Security Agency (NSA), told the BBC News Channel that the NCIC's data included "critical information relating to nationwide criminal activity" and needed to be protected.

He added that while US security agencies including the FBI have "an amazing ability" to keep such information safe" and are "globally respected", the level of cyber-attacks is rising globally.

"There's a lot of different reasons why that's happening but I do have faith in our experts in government," Lorhmann noted.

In September, the FBI remarked it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.

After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.

In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.

The USDA has not publicly commented on the concern.

#138840. Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (633 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (633 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.
  • According to recent reports, you don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones.
  • A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.

According to recent reports, you don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones. If your computer or laptop's headphone jack already delivers clean audio at a comfortable volume, then you're probably fine. Some MacBooks from 2021 and later, for example, support both low- and high-impedance headphones and can deliver up to 3 volts RMS through their headphone jacks when you use headphones rated between 150 and 1,000 ohms. If your headphone jack isn't quite as capable, or if you're not satisfied with the sound, though, then it's time to spend on some hardware.

A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units. And while the latter seems like the more serious setup, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll enjoy a better listening experience. The main job of a DAC is to turn digital audio signals into analog signals, while the amplifier takes those analog signals and makes them loud enough to power your headphones. Both a DAC/amp combo and a stack do the same thing, and which you go for largely depends on your headphones, how much flexibility you need and, of course, your budget.

It has been revealed that for most listeners, a DAC/amp is the way to go, especially if you're trying to improve your computer's audio without taking up too much space. Not only is a single unit more convenient, but it also means fewer cables dangling around and one less power adapter to worry about. You can even use a portable USB-C DAC/amp dongle designed for smartphones, but desktop versions usually offer better connectivity and power.

Industry observers note that DAC/amps can also offer better value than separates, too. Schiit's Magni 6 sells for $169 with its optional internal USB DAC. Conversely, you can buy the Magni 6 sans DAC for $99 and pair it with the Modi 5 DAC for $149 (or $164 with a power adapter). That brings the total to over $250, and you don't even get an interconnect cable. The Modi 5 has optical and coaxial inputs, sure, but that doesn't automatically equate to better sound.

DAC/amp combos don't necessarily have to come with major compromises, either. The $549 JDS Labs Element IV delivers up to 3.2 watts per channel into 32 ohms, and comes with features like automatic gain switching, EQ and even preamp outputs for powered speakers. That's more than enough for many demanding headphones, eliminating the need for a dedicated amplifier. The downside, of course, is that you're stuck with the combo and can't upgrade piecemeal.

Recent findings suggest that while DAC/amp combos are great, a stack can still make sense for audiophiles who use a wide variety of headphones or who like to tinker with their hi-fi setup. Going with separates gives you the freedom to upgrade the amplifier down the line without giving up a perfectly capable DAC, or vice versa.

Certain headphones may also benefit from the power a dedicated amp can provide. Some high-impedance headphones just ask for a lot of power, while planar magnetic models, for example, can combine low impedance and low sensitivity. Let's take the HiFiMAN Susvara Unveiled, for example, which has a 45-ohm impedance and only 86 dB sensitivity. The Absolute Sound advises at least 6 watts of amplification, so a standalone amp may be the better choice here. However, too much power can be a bad thing, too: a very powerful amp may result in audible hiss with very sensitive headphones. So start by checking your headphones' power requirements and the amplifier's noise performance instead of just assuming that you need a beefy amp.

French minister under fire for Playboy magazine cover

💡 Key Takeaways
  • French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.
  • In a recent development, schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights.
  • Schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

French government minister Marlene Schiappa has come under fire from members of her own party after appearing on the front cover of Playboy magazine.

In a recent development, schiappa, who has been a government minister since 2017, appeared on the cover of the magazine to accompany a 12-page interview she did on women’s and LGBT rights. Schiappa, who is the current Minister for the Social Economy and French Associations, was photographed for the cover wearing a white dress.

Schiappa has been a long-time advocate for women’s rights and was appointed as the country’s first ever Gender Equality Minister in 2017. In this role, she successfully spearheaded a upcoming sexual harassment law which allows for on the spot fines to be issued to men who catcall, harass or follow women on the street.

Her appearance has drawn criticism from political colleagues including French Prime Minister Elisabeth Borne.

Borne pulled up Schiappa over the cover, telling her it “wasn’t appropriate, especially during this period,” CNN affiliate BFMTV reported Saturday, citing a source close to the prime minister.

France is right now in the throes of a political and social crisis triggered by French President Emmanuel Macron’s move to push ahead with controversial pension reforms despite widespread public opposition.

“We are in the middle of a social crisis, there is the issue of policing, there are people between life and death, and I have the impression of being behind a smoke screen,” Sandrine Rousseau, Green Party politician and fellow women’s rights activist, told BFMTV Friday.

France wracked by more pension protests amid rising violence on the streets.

French politician, Jean Luc Mélenchon who came third in the 2022 presidential elections criticized both Schiappa’s appearance and the decision by French President Emmanuel Macron to give an interview to children’s magazine, Pif Gadget, this week.

Sources indicate that “In a country where the President expresses himself in Pif and his minister in Playboy, the problem would be the opposition. France is going off the rails,” Mélenchon tweeted Saturday.

Schiappa responded to her critics in a tweet on Saturday, saying: “Defending the right of women to have control of their bodies, that’s everywhere and all the time. In France, women are free. With all due respect to the detractors and hypocrites.”.

French Interior Minister, Gérald Darmanin came to Schiappa’s defense during an interview with French news channel CNews on Sunday calling her a “woman of character.”.

“I wanted to say that Marlene Schiappa is a courageous female politician who has her character and who has her style which is not mine, but I respect,” he remarked.

SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S.
  • Sources indicate that CNN first reported the letter’s existence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

Recent findings suggest that “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

Sources indicate that CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

Sources indicate that on October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has noted that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

The communications from Himes suggest that congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

In a recent development, it seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the tech giant is presently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.
